Hoppscotch device-login open redirect token theft via localhost.* / sslip.io bypass AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to Hoppscotch's /device-login endpoint where the redirect_uri parameter abuses the flawed startsWith('http://localhost') validation by using localhost.<attacker-domain> or localhost.<ip>.sslip.io to exfiltrate session tokens. Detects GHSA-7fg7-wx5q-6m3v exploitation in versions <= 2026.2.1. Rationale: Anchored on the exact bypass primitives the article documents: redirect_uri=http://localhost.<attacker>/ and the sslip.io payload (http://localhost.<attacker-ip>.sslip.io/) the Aikido agents used to verify the flaw. The startsWith('http://localhost') check passes any subdomain of an attacker-controlled domain — these two substrings are the highest-fidelity signal because legitimate device-login uses bare http://localhost/device-token. Cross-referenced GHSA-7fg7-wx5q-6m3v and PR #6012. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/hoppscotch/hoppscotch/pull/6012 • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10462
ATT&CKT1539 T1190 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal QA testing the device-login flow with deliberately malformed URIs
  • Hoppscotch developer running an integration test that points redirect_uri to a localhost.localdomain DNS suffix
  • Pentesters or red-team exercises probing the patched build to confirm regression coverage
  • Security-research traffic from approved scanners hitting the test endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not(csUriQuery matches regex @"redirect_uri=https?(:|%3A)(/|%2F){2}localhost(:|%3A|/|%2F)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full URL and the upstream Referer/UserAgent; resolve the redirect_uri domain — sslip.io subdomains and any localhost.<external-domain> are immediate red flags. Identify the victim user via session cookie or csUserName. 2) Contain: invalidate the victim's Hoppscotch session tokens server-side, force re-authentication, and block the attacker-controlled domain at the proxy/firewall. Confirm the instance has been upgraded to >= 2026.3.0. 3) Hunt: pivot on the victim's account for any post-token activity in the last 24h (mock-server modifications, collection moves, GraphQL mutations from unfamiliar IPs); search inbound mail/chat for the phishing link that delivered the URL.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "/device-login"
| where RemoteUrl contains "redirect_uri"
| where RemoteUrl contains "localhost." or RemoteUrl contains "sslip.io"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem contains "/device-login"
| where csUriQuery contains "redirect_uri"
| where csUriQuery contains "localhost." or csUriQuery contains "sslip.io"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csUserName, scStatus
title: Hoppscotch device-login open redirect token theft
id: 7a4b3c2d-1e5f-4a6b-9c8d-0e1f2a3b4c5d
description: Detects requests to Hoppscotch /device-login with redirect_uri pointing to localhost.* subdomains or sslip.io patterns, exploiting GHSA-7fg7-wx5q-6m3v in versions <= 2026.2.1.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/ai-pentest-hoppscotch-vulnerabilities
  - https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10462
  - https://github.com/hoppscotch/hoppscotch/pull/6012
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/04/08
tags:

  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/device-login'
  selection_query:
    cs-uri-query|contains: 'redirect_uri'

    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'localhost.'

| DomainName=/(^localhost\.[a-z0-9\-]+|\.sslip\.io$)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())

Hoppscotch Mock Server stored XSS via GraphQL updateRESTUserRequest content-type override AIExploitation Medium
Hunts GraphQL traffic invoking the updateRESTUserRequest mutation with a response body that sets Content-Type:text/html and embeds script-bearing markup, then correlates with subsequent GET requests to /mock/<subdomain>/ from the same client. Detects GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v exploitation against versions <= 2026.2.1. Rationale: Targets the exact mutation name the article cites (updateRESTUserRequest) plus the malicious payload shape — a response header object with key:content-type and value:text/html paired with an XSS-bearing body (<img src=x onerror=...>). The Sentinel query uses a same-source-IP correlation between a /graphql POST and a subsequent /mock/ GET because Hoppscotch's mock URLs sit at /mock/<subdomain>/ and rendering them is what triggers the planted script. WAF body inspection (Datadog @http.body) gives the cleanest single-event signal. Cross-referenced GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v and PR #6006. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/hoppscotch/hoppscotch/pull/6006 • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10463
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1190 T1185
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users updating mock-server responses via the official UI and then previewing them
  • Hoppscotch self-hosted demo / training environments where mock endpoints are exercised heavily
  • Automated end-to-end tests (Cypress, Playwright) hitting GraphQL then the rendered mock URL
  • Developers iterating on a mock that legitimately returns HTML for a webhook simulation
  • API consumers polling mock endpoints from headless browsers
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the GraphQL POST body via the WAF and confirm a content-type:text/html header is present in the responses[] block plus an onerror/<script> payload; note the mutation's request ID and the originating user. 2) Contain: revert the malicious mock-server response via DB rollback or admin UI, invalidate any sessions that visited the /mock/<id>/ URL, and force CSP enforcement (PR #6006). Confirm the instance is upgraded to >= 2026.3.0. 3) Hunt: enumerate every account that fetched the affected /mock/ path in the last 7 days, pivot to their post-visit GraphQL activity for token misuse or collection edits, and review any data the XSS payload could have exfiltrated (collection bodies, environment variables, API keys).
let GraphqlPosts = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains "/graphql"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","curl.exe","python.exe","node.exe")
    | project GraphqlTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, GraphqlUrl=RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "/mock/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari.exe")
| join kind=inner GraphqlPosts on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (GraphqlTime .. GraphqlTime + 24h)
| project Timestamp, GraphqlTime, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, MockUrl=RemoteUrl, GraphqlUrl
let GraphqlPosts = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem contains "/graphql"
    | where csMethod == "POST"
    | project GraphqlTime=TimeGenerated, GraphqlIP=cIP, GraphqlUser=csUserName, GraphqlStem=csUriStem;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem startswith "/mock/"
| where csMethod == "GET"
| join kind=inner GraphqlPosts on $left.cIP == $right.GraphqlIP
| where TimeGenerated between (GraphqlTime .. GraphqlTime + 24h)
| project TimeGenerated, GraphqlTime, Computer, cIP, csUserName, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus, GraphqlStem
source:nginx @http.method:POST @http.url:*/graphql* @http.body:(*updateRESTUserRequest* AND (*text/html* OR *onerror* OR *<script* OR *javascript\:*))

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as graphqlTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/graphql*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src Web.user Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| join type=inner src [
    | tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as mockTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/mock/*" Web.http_method=GET by Web.src Web.url Web.http_user_agent

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| join type=inner src [
    | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as mockTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/mock/*" Web.http_method=GET by Web.src Web.url Web.http_user_agent
    | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
    | rename url as mockUrl http_user_agent as mockUA
  ]
| where mockTime >= graphqlTime AND mockTime <= graphqlTime + 86400

Hoppscotch cross-team request injection via moveRequest GraphQL with null nextRequestID AIExploitation Medium
Hunts GraphQL POSTs invoking the MoveTeamRequest mutation where the nextRequestID variable is null and the destCollID belongs to a team the actor is not a member of, exploiting the missing GqlCollectionTeamMemberGuard check. Targets GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v exploitation in versions <= 2026.2.1. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim operationName (MoveTeamRequest) and the precise exploit primitive the article documents — variables.next set to null while destCollID points to a victim team's collection. The article calls out that nextRequestID:null causes the backend to skip the destination team check, so the null literal is the high-fidelity signal. Detection requires HTTP body capture; Sentinel uses CommonSecurityLog.Message (the WAF body sink) and Datadog uses @http.body. EDR (Defender DeviceProcessEvents, Falcon FDR) doesn't see GraphQL payloads so those slots are intentionally empty. Cross-referenced GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v. Cross-checked against: • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10461
ATT&CKT1190 T1213 T1199
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users moving a request to the end of a collection they own (nextRequestID is naturally null in that case)
  • Bulk-import scripts or migration tools repositioning requests via the GraphQL API
  • Hoppscotch admins reorganising collections after a team merge
  • Automated end-to-end tests exercising the move workflow
  • CI pipelines that rebuild collections from source-controlled API definitions
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the requestID, destCollID, and acting user from the WAF body; query the Hoppscotch DB to confirm whether the source request's teamID differs from the destination collection's teamID — if it does, this is the cross-tenant violation the article describes. 2) Contain: revert the move by issuing a corrective moveRequest back to the original collection, audit and revoke any API keys or auth headers embedded in the moved request, and force the instance upgrade to >= 2026.3.0. Notify the impacted team. 3) Hunt: enumerate every moveRequest mutation in the last 30d, join against the team/collection ownership tables, and surface every mutation where source.teamID != destCollection.teamID — these are confirmed exploitation events. Review any subsequent requests run against the injected payload that could have exfiltrated auth headers or variables.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL contains "/graphql"
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where Message contains "MoveTeamRequest" or Message contains "moveRequest"
| where Message contains "nextRequestID" or Message contains "\"next\":null"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
source:nginx @http.method:POST @http.url:*/graphql* @http.body:(*MoveTeamRequest* OR *moveRequest*) @http.body:*destCollID* @http.body:(*"next":null* OR *nextRequestID*)
WEB
index=* (sourcetype=nginx:plus:access OR sourcetype=hoppscotch:* OR sourcetype=waf:*)
  uri_path="*/graphql*" http_method=POST
  ("MoveTeamRequest" OR "moveRequest")
  "nextRequestID" "null"
  destCollID
| rex field=_raw "\"req\"\s*:\s*\"(?<reqId>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "\"dest\"\s*:\s*\"(?<destCollId>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "\"next\"\s*:\s*(?<nextVal>null|\"[^\"]*\")"
| where nextVal="null"
| stats count, values(reqId) as movedRequestIds, values(destCollId) as destCollIds, dc(destCollId) as uniqueDests, earliest(_time) as first, latest(_time) as last by src, user
| where count >= 1

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

IoliteLabs VSCode extension dropper: VS Code child process reaching rraghh.com / oortt.com C2 AIDelivery High
Detects the obfuscated pako/index.js dropper inside the malicious IoliteLabs Solidity extensions spawning curl/cmd to fetch stage-2 from the attacker's C2 infrastructure. Fires on any child of VS Code, Code Insiders, Cursor, Windsurf, or VSCodium whose command line references rraghh.com, cdn.rraghh.com, or oortt.com — the three exclusive domains used by this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three campaign-exclusive C2 hostnames (rraghh.com, cdn.rraghh.com, oortt.com) confirmed in both the StepSecurity disclosure and the public GitHub issue #4 on iolitelabs/vscode-solidity-iolite. The parent-process narrowing to the VS Code family (incl. Cursor / Windsurf / VSCodium) ensures we hit only dropper executions and not analyst lookups of these strings in browsers/editors. Activation event onStartupFinished means this fires on every IDE launch on a compromised host, so a 30d lookback will catch any historic infection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-iolitelabs-vscode-extensions-target-solidity-developers-on-windows-macos-and-linux-with-backdoor • https://github.com/iolitelabs/vscode-solidity-iolite/issues/4 • https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=IoliteLabs.solidity-windows • https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=IoliteLabs.solidity-macos
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","Code - Insiders.exe","Cursor.exe","Windsurf.exe","VSCodium.exe","Positron.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Microsoft VS Code\", @"\Cursor\", @"\Windsurf\", @"\VSCodium\")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rraghh.com","oortt.com","cdn.rraghh.com")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"%TEMP%\1.bat", @"\Temp\1.bat"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Code.exe","Code - Insiders.exe","Cursor.exe","Windsurf.exe","VSCodium.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("rraghh.com","oortt.com","cdn.rraghh.com")
   or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "curl" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "\\1.bat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IoliteLabs Stage-2 regsvr32 LOLbin loading ntuser DLL from fake Chrome\ChromeUpdate path AIInstallation High
Detects the 7WhiteSmoke.msi stage-2 installer's execution of regsvr32 against an extension-less file named 'ntuser' under %APPDATA%\Chrome\ChromeUpdate\ — the persistence + DLL-load technique used by the IoliteLabs backdoor. The combination of regsvr32 LOLbin + ntuser file + fake ChromeUpdate path + DllInstall (-i flag) is extremely article-specific and avoids generic regsvr32 detections. Rationale: The combination is uniquely article-specific: regsvr32 /s /i is one DLL-load LOLbin variant, but the path '\Chrome\ChromeUpdate\ntuser' is a deliberate masquerade chosen by this attacker (per the StepSecurity OLE2/cabinet analysis) — Google's real Chrome updater is GoogleUpdate / msedge_updater, never under that path. We also pin the SHA256 of the dropper DLL (5f9c09c2c432a6b94f2200455065bcfd1237f8a01b913a7c9e37f164ff99a84c) and the MSI installer (e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3) for file-event matching. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-iolitelabs-vscode-extensions-target-solidity-developers-on-windows-macos-and-linux-with-backdoor • https://github.com/iolitelabs/vscode-solidity-iolite/issues/4
ATT&CKT1218.010 T1036.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let _knownHashes = dynamic(["5f9c09c2c432a6b94f2200455065bcfd1237f8a01b913a7c9e37f164ff99a84c","e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3"]);
let ProcSig = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "regsvr32.exe"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "ntuser"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Chrome\ChromeUpdate"
         or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)regsvr32(\.exe)?\s+/s\s+/i\s+.*ntuser"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="ProcessExec";
let HashSig = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 in (_knownHashes)
       or (FileName =~ "ntuser" and FolderPath has @"\Chrome\ChromeUpdate")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=tostring(SHA256), Source="FileWrite";
union ProcSig, HashSig
| order by Timestamp desc
let _knownHashes = dynamic(["5f9c09c2c432a6b94f2200455065bcfd1237f8a01b913a7c9e37f164ff99a84c","e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3"]);
let ProcSig = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith @"\regsvr32.exe"
    | where CommandLine has "ntuser"
    | where CommandLine has @"\Chrome\ChromeUpdate"
         or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)regsvr32(\.exe)?\s+/s\s+/i\s+.*ntuser"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source="SecurityEvent4688";
let AsimSig = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetProcessName endswith @"\regsvr32.exe"
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has "ntuser" and TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\Chrome\ChromeUpdate"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source="ImProcessCreate";
let FileSig = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFileSHA256 in (_knownHashes)
       or (TargetFileName =~ "ntuser" and TargetFilePath has @"\Chrome\ChromeUpdate")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName=ActingProcessName, Source="ImFileEvent";
union ProcSig, AsimSig, FileSig
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: IoliteLabs Backdoor - regsvr32 LOLbin Loading ntuser DLL from Fake Chrome ChromeUpdate Path
id: 9b3c5e72-8a4f-4d1c-b6e9-7c2a1d8f5e93
status: experimental
description: Detects the IoliteLabs stage-2 backdoor's persistence/load technique where regsvr32 is invoked with /s /i flags against an extension-less 'ntuser' file under %APPDATA%\Chrome\ChromeUpdate\. The MSI installer (7WhiteSmoke.msi) masquerades as a Chrome browser updater and ships this DLL containing SetDesktopMonitorHook / ClearDesktopMonitorHook exports.
references:
    - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-iolitelabs-vscode-extensions-target-solidity-developers-on-windows-macos-and-linux-with-backdoor
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/13

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="regsvr32.exe" AND Processes.process="*ntuser*" AND (Processes.process="*\\Chrome\\ChromeUpdate*" OR Processes.process="* /i *") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)regsvr32.*\\s/(s|i)\\b.*ntuser") OR match(process,"(?i)Chrome\\\\ChromeUpdate\\\\ntuser") | sort - firstTime
IoliteLabs IOC sweep: rraghh.com / oortt.com hostnames + campaign file hashes AICommand & Control Medium
Broad IOC-driven sweep for any host that resolves, contacts, or writes files associated with the IoliteLabs Solidity backdoor — network connections to rraghh.com / cdn.rraghh.com / oortt.com plus the four pivotal SHA-256 hashes (tampered pako, MSI installer, ntuser DLL). Use this as a retro-hunt on first deployment, and standing rule going forward. Rationale: All four IOCs (three domains + three file hashes) are unique to this campaign per StepSecurity's analysis and corroborated by GitHub issue #4 on the upstream IoliteLabs repository (where the project maintainers acknowledge the malicious v0.1.8 publish was outside their control). Hostnames are checked via DNS-suffix match to also catch CNAME redirections and any future subdomains under rraghh.com / oortt.com. The 7WhiteSmoke.msi filename + Documents folder write path is the second C2 hop (oortt.com) not present in the original dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-iolitelabs-vscode-extensions-target-solidity-developers-on-windows-macos-and-linux-with-backdoor • https://github.com/iolitelabs/vscode-solidity-iolite/issues/4 • https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=IoliteLabs.solidity-windows
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web Endpoint.Filesystem
let _iocHashes = dynamic(["fcd398abc51fd16e8bc93ef8d88a23d7dec28081b6dfce4b933020322a610508","e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3","5f9c09c2c432a6b94f2200455065bcfd1237f8a01b913a7c9e37f164ff99a84c"]);
let _iocDomains = dynamic(["rraghh.com","oortt.com","cdn.rraghh.com"]);
let Net = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (_iocDomains) or tostring(RemoteIP) in (_iocDomains)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Indicator=RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="Network";
let Dns = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
    | extend Q = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).QueryName)
    | where Q endswith "rraghh.com" or Q endswith "oortt.com"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Indicator=Q, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="DNS";
let Files = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 in (_iocHashes)
       or (FileName =~ "7WhiteSmoke.msi")
       or (FileName =~ "1.bat" and FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\"))
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Indicator=strcat(FileName," / ",SHA256), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="File";
union Net, Dns, Files
| order by Timestamp desc
let _iocHashes = dynamic(["fcd398abc51fd16e8bc93ef8d88a23d7dec28081b6dfce4b933020322a610508","e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3","5f9c09c2c432a6b94f2200455065bcfd1237f8a01b913a7c9e37f164ff99a84c"]);
let _iocDomains = dynamic(["rraghh.com","oortt.com","cdn.rraghh.com"]);
let Web = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Url has_any (_iocDomains) or DstHostname has_any (_iocDomains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Indicator=Url, Source="WebSession";
let Dns = ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery endswith "rraghh.com" or DnsQuery endswith "oortt.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Indicator=DnsQuery, Source="DNS";
let Files = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFileSHA256 in (_iocHashes)
       or TargetFileName =~ "7WhiteSmoke.msi"
       or (TargetFileName =~ "1.bat" and TargetFilePath has "\\Temp\\")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, Indicator=strcat(TargetFileName," / ",TargetFileSHA256), Source="File";
union Web, Dns, Files
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fcd398abc51fd16e8bc93ef8d88a23d7dec28081b6dfce4b933020322a610508", "e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3") or SHA1 in~ ("fcd398abc51fd16e8bc93ef8d88a23d7dec28081b6dfce4b933020322a610508", "e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3") or MD5 in~ ("fcd398abc51fd16e8bc93ef8d88a23d7dec28081b6dfce4b933020322a610508", "e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fcd398abc51fd16e8bc93ef8d88a23d7dec28081b6dfce4b933020322a610508", "e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3") or SHA1 in~ ("fcd398abc51fd16e8bc93ef8d88a23d7dec28081b6dfce4b933020322a610508", "e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3") or MD5 in~ ("fcd398abc51fd16e8bc93ef8d88a23d7dec28081b6dfce4b933020322a610508", "e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fcd398abc51fd16e8bc93ef8d88a23d7dec28081b6dfce4b933020322a610508", "e903ae267bf7ed1d02b218c1dc7cf6d87257e87de9fbda411a13f9154716bfa3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TeamPCP Plants WAV Steganography Credential Stealer in telnyx PyPI Package

StepSecurity
2026-04-02 12 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On March 27, 2026, TeamPCP injected a WAV steganography-based credential stealer into two releases of the telnyx Python SDK on PyPI. The issue was disclosed in team-telnyx/telnyx-python#235. TeamPCP is the same group behind the litellm supply chain compromise three days earlier, identified by a shared RSA-4096 public key, identical encryption scheme, and the tpcp.tar.gz exfiltration signature present in both attacks.

TeamPCP telnyx FetchAudio() — python subprocess running inline base64 exec AIInstallation High
Detects the FetchAudio() module-level trigger from telnyx 4.87.1/4.87.2 supply-chain compromise: spawns a detached `python -c "import base64; exec(base64.b64decode('...').decode())"` subprocess that decodes the embedded `_p` blob and runs the Linux/macOS credential harvester. The exact cmdline shape (literal `import base64; exec(base64.b64decode(`) is article-specific and was emitted verbatim by the malicious _client.py. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim `subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", f"import base64; exec(base64.b64decode('{_p}').decode())"])` shape shown in the article's FetchAudio() body — this exact one-liner is the only execution vector used to detonate the Linux/macOS payload, so the dual-keyword cmdline match is high-fidelity for this campaign and other PyPI stealers using the same `_p` blob trick. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/team-telnyx/telnyx-python/issues/235 • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/teampcp-plants-wav-steganography-credential-stealer-in-telnyx-pypi-package
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1027.013 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD runners (GitHub Actions, GitLab Runners) executing base64-encoded inline Python from job env-vars
  • Ansible/SaltStack modules transferring base64-packed Python payloads to managed hosts
  • Internal RPA tooling that wraps secrets/scripts in base64 before exec
  • Penetration-testing frameworks (e.g. Impacket helpers) using the same one-liner shape
  • Pyinstaller / PyOxidizer bootstrap shims (rare on Linux/macOS production hosts)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("ansible-playbook","salt-minion","runner.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible_module","salt-call"))
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName == "Runner.Worker.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "GITHUB_ACTIONS")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent chain for the python process — if the grandparent is `pip` or the immediate ancestor imported `telnyx`, treat as confirmed TeamPCP detonation; capture the `_p` blob from the cmdline for IR. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached python session (`start_new_session=True` means it survives the parent app), rotate every credential, SSH key, env-var secret, and cloud token reachable from that host — assume full credential compromise per StepSecurity guidance. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host's outbound connections to 83.142.209.203:8080, search the fleet for telnyx 4.87.1/4.87.2 installs (`pip freeze` + sbom), and check for tpcp.tar.gz file artefacts on any host where the harvester ran.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "import base64" and ProcessCommandLine has "exec(base64.b64decode"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","python3.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","python3.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "import telnyx"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "import base64" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "exec(base64.b64decode"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection to TeamPCP C2 83.142.209.203 / ringtone.wav stego payload fetch AICommand & Control High
Detects the urllib.request fetch to `http://83.142.209.203:8080/ringtone.wav` performed by the audioimport() payload after the FetchAudio() subprocess decodes `_p`. The IP+port+path is unique to the TeamPCP telnyx campaign and shared with the litellm compromise three days earlier (same RSA-4096 key, same exfil signature). Rationale: Anchored on the literal IOC pair from the article: IP `83.142.209.203` on port 8080, GET path `/ringtone.wav`, fetched via urllib.request with `Mozilla/5.0` User-Agent. The IP is unique to TeamPCP infrastructure (StepSecurity ties it to the litellm campaign via shared RSA-4096 key + tpcp.tar.gz exfil signature), so any contact is essentially a confirmed campaign hit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/teampcp-plants-wav-steganography-credential-stealer-in-telnyx-pypi-package • https://github.com/team-telnyx/telnyx-python/issues/235

msbuild.exe dropped to Startup folder (TeamPCP telnyx Windows persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects the Windows persistence step from the telnyx 4.87.2 setup() function — a binary masquerading as `msbuild.exe` written to the user's Startup folder (`%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\msbuild.exe`). Legitimate msbuild.exe ships under Program Files or the .NET SDK install dirs, never Startup. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit persistence mechanism: `setup()` (the Windows branch of the attack) drops a binary disguised as `msbuild.exe` into the Startup folder. The legitimate msbuild.exe never lives in `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\` — it ships in `C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\` or `C:\Program Files\dotnet\sdk\` — so a name+path match is essentially zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/teampcp-plants-wav-steganography-credential-stealer-in-telnyx-pypi-package • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing a build automation script that intentionally autoruns msbuild on logon (extremely rare; usually a .lnk, not the binary itself)
  • Endpoint imaging tools restoring a Startup-folder snapshot containing legacy items
  • Malware sandbox VM detonating the package for analysis
  • Red-team / purple-team exercise dropping the same artefact
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Microsoft Visual Studio")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped msbuild.exe and compare against the legitimate Microsoft.Build.dll-signed msbuild — TeamPCP's copy is unsigned or self-signed and will not match any official MS publisher; pull the writer process which should trace back to a Python session that imported telnyx. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the Startup entry, kill any running impostor msbuild.exe, rotate all credentials reachable from that host. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same file path, pivot to the file's outbound connections (should beacon back to TeamPCP infrastructure), and check for the litellm-campaign sibling IOCs (tpcp.tar.gz, RSA-4096 public key references in modules).

| where FolderPath has @"\Startup\"
   or FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
   or FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the writer process and parent chain for the tpcp.tar.gz write — should trace back to a python interpreter session that imported telnyx (or another TeamPCP-compromised package). Hash the archive and check for the litellm/telnyx campaign overlap. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, kill the Python session, block egress to 83.142.209.203, and rotate every credential that lived on the host — environment variables, SSH keys, cloud SDK profiles, browser keychain entries. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same filename, look for FetchAudio-shaped python cmdlines on the same host in the preceding 60 minutes, and review network egress to identify whether the archive was already shipped before isolation.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "tpcp.tar.gz"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp asc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "tpcp.tar.gz"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated asc

pip install of malicious telnyx versions 4.87.1 / 4.87.2 AIDelivery High
Detects installation of the two compromised telnyx PyPI releases (4.87.1 and 4.87.2) via pip — the supply-chain inflection point before any other detection in this campaign fires. Either explicit version pinning or a `pip install --upgrade telnyx` that resolves to the bad release. Rationale: Anchored on the article's two named malicious versions (4.87.1 and 4.87.2) of the telnyx PyPI package — the only releases that contain the FetchAudio/setup payloads. The last clean release was 4.87.0. A pip install matching both the package name AND one of those exact versions is a confirmed supply-chain compromise event with no legitimate use case. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/teampcp-plants-wav-steganography-credential-stealer-in-telnyx-pypi-package • https://github.com/team-telnyx/telnyx-python/issues/235 • https://pypi.org/project/telnyx/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Reverse-engineering / detection-engineering team intentionally installing 4.87.1 or 4.87.2 in a sandbox for IOC extraction
  • SBOM vulnerability scanner that replays installs to confirm presence
  • Developer pinning to the bad version while testing a rollback
  • Penetration testers reproducing the campaign in a tabletop
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox-","sbx-","malware-vm","sbom-scanner") or AccountName has_any ("sbom","vulnscan","threathunter","redteam"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, user account, and parent shell that ran pip; check whether `import telnyx` has been executed since (DeviceProcessEvents for python with subsequent FetchAudio cmdline, or DeviceNetworkEvents to 83.142.209.203). If yes, treat as detonated. 2) Contain: uninstall the package (`pip uninstall telnyx`), pin to 4.87.0 or revert to the latest clean release, isolate the host if detonation is confirmed, and rotate every credential reachable from the box (env-vars, SSH keys, cloud creds, browser-stored tokens) per StepSecurity remediation guidance. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same pip install pattern, search for tpcp.tar.gz, msbuild.exe in Startup folders, and outbound connections to 83.142.209.203 over the past 30 days; flag any CI runner / container image that pulled the bad versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where (FileName has_any ("pip","pip3","pip.exe","pip3.exe"))
   or (FileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","python3.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "-m pip")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "telnyx"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("4.87.1","4.87.2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where (ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","pip.exe","pip3.exe"))
   or (ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-m pip")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "telnyx"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("4.87.1","4.87.2")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Installation of Malicious telnyx PyPI Package (4.87.1 / 4.87.2)
id: a5ecf728-b19a-4c2e-df60-5c6b7f8e9fa0
status: experimental
description: Detects pip install of the compromised telnyx 4.87.1 or 4.87.2 PyPI releases backdoored by TeamPCP with a WAV-steganography credential stealer.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/03/27

logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_pip:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/pip'
      - '/pip3'
      - '\\pip.exe'
      - '\\pip3.exe'
  selection_pymodule:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'

      - 'install'
      - 'telnyx'
  selection_version:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '4.87.1'
      - '4.87.2'

  - SBOM / vulnerability scanner replaying installs in a sandbox
level: high

(source:linux.auditd OR source:windows.sysmon OR source:windows.security) (@process.command_line:(*"pip install"* AND *telnyx* AND (*4.87.1* OR *4.87.2*)) OR @CommandLine:(*"pip install"* AND *telnyx* AND (*4.87.1* OR *4.87.2*)) OR @CommandLine:(*"-m pip"* AND *install* AND *telnyx* AND (*4.87.1* OR *4.87.2*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/pip(3)?(\.exe)?$/i OR (ImageFileName=/python(3)?(\.exe)?$/i AND CommandLine=/-m\s+pip/i))
| CommandLine=/install/i
| CommandLine=/telnyx/i
| CommandLine=/(4\.87\.1|4\.87\.2)/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pip","pip3","pip.exe","pip3.exe") OR Processes.process="*-m pip*") AND Processes.process="*install*" AND Processes.process="*telnyx*" AND (Processes.process="*4.87.1*" OR Processes.process="*4.87.2*") by host, user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pip","pip3","pip.exe","pip3.exe") OR Processes.process="*-m pip*") AND Processes.process="*install*" AND Processes.process="*telnyx*" AND (Processes.process="*4.87.1*" OR Processes.process="*4.87.2*") by host, user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised litellm 1.82.7 / 1.82.8 PyPI install (TeamPCP supply-chain) AIInstallation High
Hunts pip/uv/poetry installing the exact malicious LiteLLM versions published by TeamPCP on 2026-03-24 (online ~40 min before PyPI quarantine). Catches the initial-access moment before .pth persistence and credential harvesting fire. Rationale: Pivots on the two exact malicious version strings (1.82.7, 1.82.8) confirmed across Datadog Security Labs, Trend Micro, JFrog and the official LiteLLM security advisory. Hard-pin to pip/uv/poetry/python parents to keep noise off. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://docs.litellm.ai/blog/security-update-march-2026 • https://research.jfrog.com/post/litellm-compromised-teampcp/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/your-ai-stack-just-handed-over-your-root-keys-inside-the-litellm-pypi-breach.html • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/compromised-litellm-pypi-package-delivers-multi-stage-credential-stealer
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the IOC in an isolated lab VM
  • SCA tooling that reproduces the version string in a scan log (filter by tool process)
  • Internal mirror cache replaying the version string in a build pipeline scan
  • Forensic responder running `pip show litellm==1.82.8` to confirm presence (this is a wanted hit, not an FP)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("snyk.exe","snyk","trivy","trivy.exe","grype","grype.exe","safety","safety.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("scan","audit","vuln"))
Response runbook
Triage: pull `pip show litellm` and `pip index versions litellm` from the host; check the install timestamp against 2026-03-24 10:39 UTC ± 40 min window plus the post-quarantine grace period during which mirrors continued serving. Contain: isolate the host, rotate every cloud/CI/SSH/Kubernetes credential reachable from that host (assume full credential blast radius — Mercor lost source code this way), and uninstall litellm before reinstalling a known-good ≥1.82.9. Hunt: pivot on the host's network telemetry for the C2 + WAV-stager IOCs in UC3/UC4; check for the `litellm_init.pth` persistence drop in UC2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip","pip3","python","python3","uv","uv.exe","poetry","poetry.exe"))
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","uv.exe","poetry.exe"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("litellm==1.82.7","litellm==1.82.8","litellm-1.82.7","litellm-1.82.8")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("litellm==1.82.7","litellm==1.82.8","litellm-1.82.7","litellm-1.82.8")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where EventID == 4688
   | where NewProcessName endswith "\\pip.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pip3.exe"
        or NewProcessName endswith "\\python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\python3.exe"
        or NewProcessName endswith "\\uv.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\poetry.exe"
   | where CommandLine has_any ("litellm==1.82.7","litellm==1.82.8","litellm-1.82.7","litellm-1.82.8")
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=TargetUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName),
  (Syslog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where SyslogMessage has_any ("litellm==1.82.7","litellm==1.82.8","litellm-1.82.7","litellm-1.82.8")
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamPCP LiteLLM Compromised PyPI Install (1.82.7 / 1.82.8)
id: 8b3c54a1-9f2c-4e7c-a6b1-7f1d4b5a2e90
description: Detects pip/uv/poetry installing the malicious litellm 1.82.7 or 1.82.8 PyPI versions published by TeamPCP on 2026-03-24.
references:
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/
  - https://docs.litellm.ai/blog/security-update-march-2026
  - https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/your-ai-stack-just-handed-over-your-root-keys-inside-the-litellm-pypi-breach.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/21
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\uv.exe'
      - '\poetry.exe'
      - '/pip'
      - '/pip3'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/uv'
      - '/poetry'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'litellm==1.82.7'
      - 'litellm==1.82.8'
      - 'litellm-1.82.7'
      - 'litellm-1.82.8'
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
  - Forensic researcher pulling the IOC sample into a sandbox; whitelist by host
level: high
(source:windows.security OR source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd) (@CommandLine:(*litellm==1.82.7* OR *litellm==1.82.8* OR *litellm-1.82.7* OR *litellm-1.82.8*) OR @process.command_line:(*litellm==1.82.7* OR *litellm==1.82.8* OR *litellm-1.82.7* OR *litellm-1.82.8*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/(pip|pip3|python|python3|uv|poetry)(\.exe)?$/i OR ParentBaseFileName=/(pip|pip3|python|python3|uv|poetry)(\.exe)?$/i)
| regex("litellm[=\\-]1\\.82\\.(7|8)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","pip","pip3","python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","uv.exe","uv","poetry.exe","poetry")) AND (Processes.process="*litellm==1.82.7*" OR Processes.process="*litellm==1.82.8*" OR Processes.process="*litellm-1.82.7*" OR Processes.process="*litellm-1.82.8*") by host, user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
litellm_init.pth Python autoload persistence drop AIInstallation High
Hunts the creation of `litellm_init.pth` under site-packages — TeamPCP's auto-execution mechanism that fires on every Python interpreter startup, even when LiteLLM itself is never imported. Version 1.82.8's signature persistence file. Rationale: `litellm_init.pth` is the unique persistence-file artefact called out by Datadog Security Labs, SafeDep and Sonatype — Python `.pth` autoload abuse is the differentiator vs 1.82.7 (which executes via `setup.py`). High-signal, no legitimate reuse of this filename in any clean LiteLLM release. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://safedep.io/malicious-litellm-1-82-8-analysis/ • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/compromised-litellm-pypi-package-delivers-multi-stage-credential-stealer
ATT&CKT1546 T1574
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic copy of the malicious artefact into a sandbox or DFIR collection share (filter by sandbox host group)
  • SCA tool unpacking the .whl to a temp dir for inspection
  • File-system imaging utility copying a quarantined sample across paths
  • Backup software replicating a known-bad-but-quarantined file
Response runbook
Triage: cat the `.pth` and confirm it contains an `exec()` / `__import__` call (the malicious version executes a base64-decoded loader; the legit Python `.pth` files contain ONLY import lines). Contain: delete the file, then `pip uninstall litellm` and treat the host as credential-compromised — rotate ssh keys, ~/.aws, ~/.kube, ~/.docker, ~/.netrc, env-var secrets, CI runner tokens. Hunt: pivot on the writing process's later behaviour for the WAV-stager pull (UC3) and the TeamPCP C2 egress (UC4) within ±2 h of the write.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "litellm_init.pth" or FolderPath has "litellm_init.pth"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "litellm_init.pth" or TargetFilePath has "litellm_init.pth"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WAV-disguised stager pull from TeamPCP loader 83.142.209.203:8080 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the second-stage download where the .pth/setup.py loader pulls a binary disguised as a .wav file from 83.142.209.203:8080. Confirmed across Trend Micro, JFrog and Hunt.io as the canonical TeamPCP stager fetch. Rationale: Hunt.io and Trend Micro both call out 83.142.209.203:8080 as the stager-fetch endpoint with WAV-file masquerade — the IP+port+file-extension combination is high-fidelity and was not used outside this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/33k-exposed-litellm-teampcp-c2-supply-chain-attack • https://www.trendmicro.com/en/research/26/c/inside-litellm-supply-chain-compromise.html • https://research.jfrog.com/post/litellm-compromised-teampcp/

  • Internet-wide scanner (Censys, Shodan) hitting the IP — these almost never land on :8080 with a GET for a .wav file, but check
  • Security researcher reproducing the kill chain on an isolated VM
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","malware-lab","purple-team"))

Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess on the host — confirm whether it's a Python/pip interpreter (matches the attack chain) or something else (could be a different threat). Contain: block 83.142.209.203/32 at perimeter + endpoint, isolate the host, and treat as breach-confirmed if the parent is Python — proceed to full credential rotation per UC1 runbook. Hunt: pivot from this host to its outbound DNS history for the TeamPCP C2 domains in UC4 (models.litellm.cloud, checkmarx.zone) and check the file system for the .pth artefact from UC2.

TeamPCP C2 / exfil egress to models.litellm.cloud, checkmarx.zone and AS205759 nodes AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts DNS resolution or direct egress to any of the TeamPCP campaign's C2 / data-exfil endpoints: models.litellm.cloud (RSA-wrapped POST exfil), checkmarx.zone (50-min payload poll), the AdaptixC2 / Havoc backend IPs, and the trycloudflare / icp0.io rotators. These domains have no legitimate use. Rationale: All seven domains and four backend IPs are confirmed across Datadog, Hunt.io, JFrog and Sonatype as TeamPCP-exclusive infrastructure. `models.litellm.cloud` is a non-BerriAI lookalike used for AES-256/RSA-4096 POST exfil; `checkmarx.zone` is the 50-min loader-poll endpoint feeding AdaptixC2 (83.142.209.11) and Havoc (45.148.10.212). All hosted on AS205759 / Ghosty Networks bulletproof. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://hunt.io/blog/33k-exposed-litellm-teampcp-c2-supply-chain-attack • https://research.jfrog.com/post/litellm-compromised-teampcp/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/inside-litellm-supply-chain-compromise.html
