Linux user-systemd sysmon persistence drop (~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py + sysmon.service) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Linux-side persistence artefacts dropped by malicious LiteLLM: a Python implant at `~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py` registered as a user-systemd unit `~/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service`. Name choice mimics legit Microsoft Sysmon-for-Linux but the path differs. Rationale: Datadog Security Labs and Sonatype both confirm `~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py` and the user-systemd `sysmon.service` unit as the Linux persistence pair. The legit Microsoft Sysmon-for-Linux binary lives under `/opt/sysmon` or `/usr/sbin/sysmon` (never `~/.config` and never `.py`), so the path itself is the discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/compromised-litellm-pypi-package-delivers-multi-stage-credential-stealer
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1036.005 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer experimenting with a personal cron/systemd helper that happens to be named sysmon (rare; check ownership)
  • DFIR responder restoring a captured artefact to a forensic VM under ~/.config (whitelist by VM hostname)
  • Configuration-management tooling deploying an internal helper named sysmon to user space (audit whether internal Ansible/Salt roles do this)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/lib/dfir/","/opt/forensics/") or DeviceName has_any ("forensic","sandbox","dfir-vm"))
Response runbook
Triage: `systemctl --user status sysmon`, read the .py contents (the malicious version makes outbound POSTs to models.litellm.cloud / checkmarx.zone — UC4). Contain: `systemctl --user disable --now sysmon && rm -rf ~/.config/sysmon ~/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service && systemctl --user daemon-reload`; isolate the host. Hunt: walk back for the litellm 1.82.7/1.82.8 install in UC1 and forward for C2 beacons in UC4. Treat as full credential compromise (the implant harvests SSH, ~/.aws, ~/.kube, ~/.docker, ~/.netrc, env-vars).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "/.config/sysmon/" and FileName =~ "sysmon.py"
    or FolderPath has "/.config/systemd/user/" and FileName =~ "sysmon.service"
    or FolderPath endswith "/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py"
    or FolderPath endswith "/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where TargetFilePath has "/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py" or TargetFilePath has "/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
  (Syslog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where SyslogMessage has_any ("/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py","/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service","systemctl --user enable sysmon","systemctl --user start sysmon")
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage, Facility)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kubernetes privileged-pod DaemonSet fan-out from compromised LiteLLM workload AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation step where the TeamPCP LiteLLM payload creates privileged pods on every node in a cluster to establish persistence and lateral movement. Pivots on K8s audit logs for create-pod/daemonset events with privileged/hostNetwork/hostPID flags and ≥3 node fan-out from a single principal. Rationale: Datadog Security Labs and Trend Micro both describe the LiteLLM 1.82.8 payload's Kubernetes module creating privileged pods on every node for persistence. The cross-node fan-out (NodesTouched ≥ 3) from one user combined with privileged/hostNetwork/hostPID flags is the article-specific signal — distinguishes from legit DaemonSets (CSI drivers, log shippers) by combining principal-novelty triage downstream. Defender and Falcon left empty because K8s control-plane audit isn't shipped to MDE/FDR in standard configs. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/inside-litellm-supply-chain-compromise.html • https://futuresearch.ai/blog/litellm-pypi-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1610 T1611 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit DaemonSet rollout: CSI driver (`csi-node`), CNI agent (`cilium`, `calico-node`), log shipper (`fluent-bit`, `datadog-agent`), security agent (`falcon-sensor`)
  • Cluster admin manually creating a debug privileged pod on each node for troubleshooting
  • Helm upgrade of a privileged add-on (cert-manager webhook, ingress-nginx in privileged mode)
  • kured / node-maintenance operators that create per-node helper pods
Suppression filter
| where not (Username has_any ("system:serviceaccount:kube-system","system:serviceaccount:kube-public","system:serviceaccount:datadog","system:serviceaccount:falcon","system:serviceaccount:cilium","system:serviceaccount:calico-system") or Namespace in ("kube-system","kube-public","gke-system"))
Response runbook
Triage: pull the RequestObject and check the container image — if it's an unfamiliar registry / contains `litellm` / matches the TeamPCP IOC images, treat as confirmed. Check the principal — is it a service account that should be allowed to create privileged pods? Contain: revoke the principal's token (`kubectl delete secret <sa-token>` + rotate), apply a Kyverno/OPA-Gatekeeper policy blocking privileged: true outside system namespaces, and `kubectl delete daemonset/pods` matching the IOC labels. Hunt: walk back to the source pod — did one of its containers run `pip install litellm` (UC1)? Pull its egress logs for the C2 IOCs in UC4.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb in ("create","patch")
| extend Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Name = tostring(ObjectRef.name)
| where Resource in ("pods","daemonsets")
| extend RO = tostring(RequestObject)
| where RO has_any ('"privileged":true','"hostNetwork":true','"hostPID":true','"hostIPC":true')
| extend NodeName = extract(@'"nodeName"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"', 1, RO)
| summarize NodesTouched = dcount(NodeName), Pods = make_set(Name, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Sample = any(RO)
            by Username, Namespace, Resource
| where NodesTouched >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR patch) @objectRef.resource:(pods OR daemonsets) (@requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostNetwork:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostPID:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostIPC:true)
CLOUD
index=k8s_audit sourcetype IN ("kube:apiserver:audit","aws:eks:audit","gcp:gke:audit") verb IN ("create","patch") objectRef.resource IN ("pods","daemonsets")
| spath input=requestObject path=spec.containers{}.securityContext.privileged output=privileged_arr
| spath input=requestObject path=spec.hostNetwork output=hostNet
| spath input=requestObject path=spec.hostPID output=hostPid
| spath input=requestObject path=spec.nodeName output=nodeName
| where 'privileged_arr'="true" OR hostNet="true" OR hostPid="true"
| stats dc(nodeName) as NodesTouched, values(objectRef.name) as Pods, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime by user.username, objectRef.namespace
| where NodesTouched >= 3
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

  • Security researcher manually probing the IOC for IOC validation
  • Block-list firewall denial logs (DeviceAction=Deny) — still worth reviewing source host but not a compromise per se
  • Vulnerability scanner / asset-discovery tool reaching the IOC after IOC-feed ingest
  • Legacy network appliance with cached resolver pointing to old DNS record
Suppression filter
| where ActionType != "ConnectionFailed" and ActionType != "ConnectionDenied" | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe", "vulnerabilityScanner.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess on the source host (look for node.exe / node / npm / yarn / pnpm / bun as ancestor; pivot on InitiatingProcessParentFileName chain). Pull the host's package-lock.json / yarn.lock and grep for axios@1.14.1, axios@0.30.4, plain-crypto-js@4.2.1, @qqbrowser/openclaw-qbot, @shadanai/openclaw. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device via Defender LiveResponse / EDR isolation. Block 142.11.206.73 and *.sfrclak.com at perimeter and DNS RPZ. Rotate any secrets exposed in CI/CD or developer env (NPM_TOKEN, AWS keys, GH_TOKEN, SSH keys, browser-saved creds). Step 3 — Hunt: search for follow-on indicators (%PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe, /tmp/ld.py, /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond), and broaden network search to any host that resolved sfrclak.com in the last 60 days even if no connection succeeded.
let C2Domains = dynamic(["sfrclak.com"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2IPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp asc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["sfrclak.com"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP in (C2IPs) or DestinationHostName has_any (C2Domains) or RequestURL has_any (C2Domains)
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, SourceUserName, DeviceAction),
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name has_any (C2Domains)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode),
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr in (C2IPs) or DstHostname has_any (C2Domains) or Url has_any (C2Domains)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, NetworkProtocol, Url)
| sort by TimeGenerated asc

PowerShell masquerading as Windows Terminal at %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe (Axios RAT Windows stage) AIInstallation High
Detects the Windows second-stage Axios RAT payload: a VBScript drops a copy of powershell.exe to C:\ProgramData\wt.exe (impersonating Windows Terminal) and launches it with execution-policy bypass and hidden-window flags. Legitimate Windows Terminal lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps or Program Files — never %PROGRAMDATA%. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim Windows-stage IOC from Table 2 of the article: %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe with PowerShell masquerading as Windows Terminal and execution-policy bypass. The %PROGRAMDATA% path is the discriminator — legitimate Windows Terminal ships via the Microsoft Store and resides under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps. Corroborated by Microsoft Security Blog and StepSecurity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://www.huntress.com/blog/supply-chain-compromise-axios-npm-package
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.001 T1059.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom enterprise app intentionally named wt.exe deployed to ProgramData by an SCCM package (rare — review packaging metadata)
  • Red-team / pentest engagement deploying a PowerShell beacon at this exact path
  • IT script-runner tool installed by an admin to ProgramData (verify with software inventory)
  • Malware-removal tool quarantine staging the file before deletion (look at parent — should be AV)
  • Developer self-built debugging stub mimicking the name (verify signing chain)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe") | where FolderPath !contains @"\WindowsApps\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: hash the wt.exe under %PROGRAMDATA% (SHA256 should match one of 617b67a8…, 92ff0877…, fcb81618…); pull the InitiatingProcessFileName — expect node.exe / wscript.exe / cscript.exe as ancestor, often kicked off by npm.exe / yarn.exe / pnpm.exe. Step 2 — Contain: isolate host, kill wt.exe process, quarantine the binary, block its hash org-wide, and check for the parallel scheduled task / Run key persistence. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents from this host to 142.11.206.73 or sfrclak.com, and grep the host's package-lock.json for axios@1.14.1, axios@0.30.4, or plain-crypto-js@4.2.1; rotate any secrets reachable from the developer/CI environment.
let SuspectPaths = dynamic([@"c:\programdata\wt.exe", @"%programdata%\wt.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\" and FileName =~ "wt.exe")
     or (FileName =~ "wt.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-ExecutionPolicy Bypass", "-ep bypass", "-WindowStyle Hidden", "-w hidden", "-nop", "-noprofile"))
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\" and FolderPath !contains @"\Microsoft\WindowsApps\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\" and FileName =~ "wt.exe"
    | project DeviceName, DropTime=Timestamp, DroppedBy=InitiatingProcessFileName, DroppedByCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DroppedSHA256=SHA256
  ) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspectName = "wt.exe";
let BypassTokens = dynamic(["-ExecutionPolicy Bypass", "-ep bypass", "-WindowStyle Hidden", "-w hidden", "-nop", "-noprofile"]);
union isfuzzy=true

    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688

Linux Python RAT orphaned via nohup python3 /tmp/ld.py (Axios npm payload) AIInstallation High
Detects the Linux second-stage Axios RAT payload: a Python script written to /tmp/ld.py and detached from its parent shell via `nohup python3`. The exact file path and orphan-via-nohup pattern are distinctive to the plain-crypto-js dropper. Rationale: Hard-anchored on the verbatim Linux IOC from the article: '/tmp/ld.py' Python script launched via 'nohup python3' to detach as an orphan background process. The path and the nohup-orphan pattern are unique enough that single-event match is high-fidelity. Corroborated by Huntress, Elastic Security Labs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/supply-chain-compromise-axios-npm-package • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps engineer ad-hoc placing a one-off Python script at /tmp/ld.py (rare and easily disambiguated by hash + git provenance)
  • Penetration test deliberately reproducing the IOC for detection validation
  • CI runner that uses /tmp as a scratch directory and happens to name a file ld.py (verify owner UID and ProcessTree origin)
  • DFIR responder running a reproduction sample in a contained lab
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root", "systemd") or ProcessCommandLine has "nohup"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm /tmp/ld.py exists and pull its SHA256 (compare to 617b67a8…, 92ff0877…, fcb81618…); look for the parent process tree — expect node → sh/bash → nohup python3, often launched from a CI/CD runner during npm/bun install. Step 2 — Contain: kill the orphaned python3 process (`pkill -f /tmp/ld.py`), quarantine the file, block 142.11.206.73 / sfrclak.com at perimeter, and rotate any secrets in the host's env (especially CI_JOB_TOKEN, AWS_*, NPM_TOKEN, SSH agent). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to outbound connections from the host to 142.11.206.73 on TCP/8000, search package-lock.json across all repos that build on this host for axios@1.14.1, axios@0.30.4, plain-crypto-js@4.2.1, @qqbrowser/openclaw-qbot, @shadanai/openclaw.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where DeviceName !endswith ".local" or 1==1  // applies to all OS; Linux sensor populates this table when MDE for Linux is deployed
| where (FileName in~ ("python3", "python", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12") and ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py")
     or (FileName =~ "nohup" and ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nohup" and FileName matches regex @"^python[0-9.]*$" and ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FolderPath == "/tmp/" and FileName =~ "ld.py"
    | project DeviceName, DropTime=Timestamp, DroppedBy=InitiatingProcessFileName, DroppedByCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DroppedSHA256=SHA256
  ) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DvcOs has_any ("Linux", "linux") or ActingProcessName matches regex @"/python[0-9.]*$" or ActingProcessName endswith "/nohup"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine),

    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Facility in ("authpriv", "auth", "daemon", "user")
    | where SyslogMessage has "/tmp/ld.py" and (SyslogMessage has "nohup" or SyslogMessage has "python")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage)

macOS Axios RAT daemon spoof + ad-hoc codesign of hidden /private/tmp binary AIInstallation High
Detects the macOS Axios RAT payload: the dropper writes a binary to /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond (impersonating an Apple background daemon) and, for follow-on `peinject` payloads, performs ad-hoc code signing on hidden binaries under /private/tmp (e.g. /private/tmp/.XXXXXX) with `codesign --force --deep --sign -` to bypass Gatekeeper. Rationale: Anchored on three verbatim macOS IOCs from the article body and Table 2: (1) the /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond drop path that spoofs an Apple daemon, (2) the `codesign --force --deep --sign -` ad-hoc signing primitive used to bypass Gatekeeper, and (3) the /private/tmp/.XXXXXX hidden-file staging pattern. Corroborated by Elastic Security Labs and GTIG (UNC1069). Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/axios-npm-package-compromised.html
ATT&CKT1036.004 T1553.002 T1564.001 T1059.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Apple internal/beta software writing a similarly named cache file (verify code signature on the binary)
  • Developer building a CLI tool locally and ad-hoc signing a binary they placed in /private/tmp/. — verifiable via shell history and team context
  • Reverse engineer running the sample in an isolated VM for analysis
  • Red-team engagement reproducing the macOS payload to validate detection
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Xcode", "xcodebuild", "swift")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: compute SHA256 of /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond and compare to 617b67a8…, 92ff0877…, fcb81618…; pull parent process — expect osascript → curl/python with sfrclak.com in command line. Step 2 — Contain: kill the RAT process (`launchctl kickstart` not applicable — direct `kill -9`), quarantine the daemon binary, remove any LaunchAgents/LaunchDaemons created by the RAT, block 142.11.206.73 / sfrclak.com at perimeter. Rotate keychain creds, AWS/GCP/AZ CLI tokens, npm tokens, SSH keys for the user. Step 3 — Hunt: search ImFileEvent for files written under /private/tmp/.* with subsequent codesign --sign - executions; pivot to outbound connections to 142.11.206.73 on TCP/8000; grep package-lock.json / yarn.lock / bun.lockb across the user's projects for axios@1.14.1, axios@0.30.4, plain-crypto-js@4.2.1.

title: macOS Axios npm RAT — daemon spoof + ad-hoc codesign of hidden /private/tmp binary
id: 3d7f2a5e-6187-42a9-bcef-5c9e0f1d2a34
status: experimental
description: Detects the macOS-stage Axios npm RAT — a binary written to /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond impersonating an Apple background daemon, and/or the `codesign --force --deep --sign -` ad-hoc signing of hidden binaries staged in /private/tmp prior to execution (a Gatekeeper bypass primitive used by the `peinject` C2 command).
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised-supply-chain-attack-delivers-cross-platform/
  - https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/21
tags:
  - attack.t1036.004
  - attack.t1553.002
  - attack.t1564.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: macos
detection:
  selection_codesign:
    Image|endswith: '/codesign'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '--force'
      - '--deep'
      - '--sign -'
      - '/private/tmp/.'
  condition: selection_codesign
falsepositives:
  - Developer building locally and ad-hoc signing a test binary they manually placed in /private/tmp/. — uncommon and verifiable via shell history
level: high
(source:windows.defender OR source:linux.syslog OR source:windows.sysmon) AND (@TargetFilename:"/Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond" OR @TargetFileName:"/Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond" OR @file.path:"/Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond" OR (@process.executable.path:*/codesign AND @process.command_line:*"--force --deep --sign -"* AND @process.command_line:*"/private/tmp/."*))
(#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/Library\/Caches\/com\.apple\.act\.mond$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| union({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/codesign$/i CommandLine=/--force.*--deep.*--sign\s+-/i CommandLine=/\/private\/tmp\/\.[A-Za-z0-9]+/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())})

npm/node postinstall hook spawning interpreter and reaching new C2 host (Axios-style dropper) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the supply-chain-dropper pattern made famous by Axios/plain-crypto-js: node.exe (or node on Linux/macOS) invoked as a postinstall hook spawns a script interpreter (wscript / cscript / osascript / python / sh) that within 60s establishes an outbound TCP connection to a never-before-seen public host. Catches the technique even if the IOCs rotate. Rationale: Generalises the dropper signature described in the article — npm postinstall hook (`"postinstall": "node setup.js"`) → node.exe → script interpreter / curl / nohup → outbound to attacker C2. The `node parent + scripting child + outbound to never-seen public host within 60s` chain is the structural fingerprint of the plain-crypto-js technique and similar npm dropper supply-chain attacks. Corroborated against GTIG / UNC1069 write-up describing the same pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.sans.org/blog/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise-malicious-packages-remote-access-trojan
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate package postinstall hooks (node-gyp, sharp, esbuild, puppeteer) downloading native binaries from CDN — exclude known registry/CDN hosts in `KnownRegistries`
  • Husky / Lefthook git-hook installers spawning shell to wire up hooks
  • Local dev `npm install` of telemetry SDK that phones home on first launch
  • Build container running `npm ci` and pulling binaries from a known internal Artifactory / Verdaccio mirror
  • Bun lockfile-resolve step spawning curl to fetch a missing tarball
Suppression filter
| where not(ChildCmd has_any ("node-gyp", "prebuild-install", "@sentry/cli", "esbuild", "husky", "lefthook", "sharp/install.js", "puppeteer/install.js")) | where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("registry.npmjs.org", "github.com", "objects.githubusercontent.com", "cdn.jsdelivr.net", "unpkg.com", "nodejs.org", "pnpm.io", "bun.sh"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: list the packages installed in the immediate npm/yarn/bun session (correlate ProcTime to recent package-lock.json / yarn.lock mtime, or fetch `npm ls --depth=0` output via LiveResponse). Flag any package whose postinstall hook spawned a non-node interpreter or made a network call to a non-CDN host. Step 2 — Contain: if a confirmed malicious package is identified, isolate the host, kill the spawned interpreter chain, block the destination IP/host at perimeter, and pin known-good versions in the affected repos. Step 3 — Hunt: query all developer/CI hosts for installs of the suspect package in the last 30 days, broaden to other postinstall droppers (@qqbrowser/openclaw-qbot, @shadanai/openclaw), and rotate secrets in any CI/CD environment that ran the affected install.
let Lookback = 30d;
let WindowSec = 60;
let PostInstallChildren = dynamic(["wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","python.exe","python3","python","sh","bash","osascript","nohup","curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget"]);
let KnownRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","registry.npm.taobao.org","npmjs.com","npmjs.org","yarnpkg.com","pnpm.io","bun.sh","jsdelivr.net","unpkg.com","github.com","githubusercontent.com"]);
let NodeChildren = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.exe", "npm", "yarn.exe", "yarn", "pnpm.exe", "pnpm", "bun.exe", "bun")
         or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.exe", "npm", "yarn.exe", "yarn", "pnpm.exe", "pnpm", "bun.exe", "bun")
    | where FileName in~ (PostInstallChildren)
    | project ProcTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, ChildName=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, ParentName=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessId;
let Beacons = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | where isnotempty(RemoteIP)
    | where not(RemoteUrl has_any (KnownRegistries))
    | project NetTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, NetProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, NetCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, NetPID=InitiatingProcessId, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl;
NodeChildren
| join kind=inner Beacons on DeviceId
| where NetTime between (ProcTime .. ProcTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| where ChildName =~ NetProc or ProcessId == NetPID
| project ProcTime, NetTime, DelaySec=datetime_diff('second', NetTime, ProcTime), DeviceName, AccountName, ParentName, ParentCmd, ChildName, ChildCmd, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by ProcTime desc

let WindowSec = 60;

let KnownRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","npmjs.com","npmjs.org","yarnpkg.com","pnpm.io","bun.sh","jsdelivr.net","unpkg.com","github.com","githubusercontent.com"]);

    | where ParentProcessName endswith "/node" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\npm.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/npm" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\yarn.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/yarn" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\pnpm.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/pnpm" or ParentProcessName endswith "/bun"
    | extend ChildLeaf = tolower(tostring(split(ActingProcessName, iff(ActingProcessName has "/", "/", "\\"))[-1]))
    | where ChildLeaf in (PostInstallChildren)

let Beacons = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
    | where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)

    | project NetTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, NetworkProtocol;
NodeChildren
| join kind=inner Beacons on DvcHostname
| where NetTime between (ProcTime .. ProcTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| project ProcTime, NetTime, DelaySec=datetime_diff('second', NetTime, ProcTime), DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ChildLeaf, ChildCmd, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);

                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
axios npm RAT C2 beacon to sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73:8000 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects network egress to the campaign-exclusive C2 infrastructure used by the plain-crypto-js dropper after the compromised axios@1.14.1 / axios@0.30.4 packages execute their postinstall hook. The dropper retrieves platform-specific payloads from http://sfrclak[.]com:8000/6202033 — any host contacting that IP or domain on any port is a near-zero-FP signal. Rationale: sfrclak.com and 142.11.206.73 (port 8000, URI /6202033) are unique campaign infrastructure for the plain-crypto-js RAT dropper — they have no legitimate use. Article corroborated by StepSecurity and Socket which independently published the same C2 IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised

axios RAT artifact dropped: com.apple.act.mond / wt.exe / ld.py with known SHA256 AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the three platform-specific RAT binaries dropped by plain-crypto-js@4.2.1's postinstall hook: /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond on macOS (masqueraded as Apple ACT daemon), %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe on Windows (PowerShell copy disguised as Windows Terminal), and /tmp/ld.py on Linux. Matches on both fixed hash and path patterns so it catches renamed-but-identical samples. Rationale: Drop paths are baked into the dropper code per platform (article + StepSecurity confirm identical paths), and the SHA256s give a hash-pinned signal even if attackers rename. Sigma uses 1-of-* across selections for cross-platform single-event coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let badHashes = dynamic([
  "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a",
  "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101",
  "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where SHA256 in (badHashes)
  or (FileName =~ "com.apple.act.mond" and FolderPath has @"/Library/Caches/")
  or (FileName =~ "wt.exe" and FolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData")
  or (FileName =~ "ld.py" and FolderPath =~ "/tmp/")
  or (FileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1") and FolderPath has @"\Temp\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let badHashes = dynamic([
  "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a",
  "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101",
  "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileSHA256 in (badHashes)
  or (TargetFileName =~ "com.apple.act.mond" and TargetFilePath has "/Library/Caches/")
  or (TargetFileName =~ "wt.exe" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\")
  or (TargetFilePath == "/tmp/ld.py")
  or (TargetFileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1") and TargetFilePath has @"\Temp\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PowerShell copy masqueraded as Windows Terminal in %PROGRAMDATA% running 6202033.ps1 AIInstallation High
Hunts the Windows-specific stage-2 chain of the axios RAT: plain-crypto-js's setup.js copies powershell.exe to %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe (mimicking Windows Terminal, which legitimately lives under \Program Files\WindowsApps), writes %TEMP%\6202033.vbs as a hidden launcher, and uses it to invoke %TEMP%\6202033.ps1 — a renamed-interpreter LOLbin pattern that bypasses powershell.exe-named telemetry. Rationale: Microsoft's real Windows Terminal (wt.exe) ships only under \Program Files\WindowsApps\Microsoft.WindowsTerminal_* — a wt.exe under \ProgramData\ is the exact masquerade described in the article. Pairing that with the literal 6202033 token (used as the URI path on the C2 and as the .vbs/.ps1 filename basename) and node.exe parents with plain-crypto-js/sfrclak strings keeps this scoped to the actual dropper chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData" and FileName =~ "wt.exe")
   or (InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wt.exe")
   or (FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "6202033")
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wt.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "6202033.ps1")
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd") and FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe") and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("6202033","plain-crypto-js","sfrclak") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("plain-crypto-js","setup.js")))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentFile = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildFile = FileName,
          ChildPath = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildSHA256 = SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(SecurityEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where EventID == 4688
 | where (NewProcessName endswith @"\ProgramData\wt.exe")
    or (ParentProcessName endswith @"\ProgramData\wt.exe")
    or (NewProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" and CommandLine has "6202033")
    or (NewProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe" and CommandLine has "6202033")
    or ((NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "6202033.ps1")
    or (ParentProcessName endswith @"\node.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("6202033","plain-crypto-js","sfrclak"))
 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType),
(ImProcessCreate
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where (TargetProcessName endswith @"\ProgramData\wt.exe")
    or (ParentProcessName endswith @"\ProgramData\wt.exe")
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") and TargetProcessCommandLine has "6202033")
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and TargetProcessCommandLine has "6202033.ps1")
    or (ParentProcessName has "node.exe" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("6202033","plain-crypto-js","sfrclak"))
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "ed8560c1ac7ceb6983ba995124d5917dc1a00288912387a6389296637d5f815c", "f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "ed8560c1ac7ceb6983ba995124d5917dc1a00288912387a6389296637d5f815c", "f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "ed8560c1ac7ceb6983ba995124d5917dc1a00288912387a6389296637d5f815c", "f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "ed8560c1ac7ceb6983ba995124d5917dc1a00288912387a6389296637d5f815c", "f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "ed8560c1ac7ceb6983ba995124d5917dc1a00288912387a6389296637d5f815c", "f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "ed8560c1ac7ceb6983ba995124d5917dc1a00288912387a6389296637d5f815c", "f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "ed8560c1ac7ceb6983ba995124d5917dc1a00288912387a6389296637d5f815c", "f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Python process spawning shell with TeamPCP recon chain (hostname; whoami; uname; ip addr fallback) · [LLM] Python process contacting AWS IMDS 169.254.169.254 (litellm stealer IAM credential theft) · [LLM] In-cluster Kubernetes secret enumeration with Python user-agent (litellm stealer K8s pivot) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Outbound DNS/HTTPS to TeamPCP exfil domain models.litellm.cloud (litellm PyPI compromise) AICommand & Control High
Detects any host beaconing or POSTing encrypted credential bundles to the attacker-controlled exfil domain hardcoded in litellm 1.82.7/1.82.8. Both compromised versions encode stolen creds with AES-256-CBC + RSA-4096 and curl-POST to https://models.litellm.cloud/ — a single resolution from any host is high-confidence compromise. Rationale: Anchored on the exact exfil endpoint 'https://models.litellm.cloud/' named in the StepSecurity write-up. A single resolution of this domain (no legitimate caller exists — the real project is litellm.ai) is near-zero false-positive. Corroborated by Sonatype, Datadog Security Labs, Snyk, and Aqua/Unit42 TeamPCP write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/compromised-litellm-pypi-package-delivers-multi-stage-credential-stealer • https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24518 • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://snyk.io/blog/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://docs.litellm.ai/blog/security-update-march-2026
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1573.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DFIR/IR team performing controlled detonation in a sandbox to confirm IOC (whitelist the analyst sandbox IP)
  • Threat-intel platform sinkhole resolving the IOC for tracking (e.g., abuse.ch, VirusTotal worker IPs)
  • Security awareness blog screenshot rendering — a browser loads a thumbnail referencing the domain string (low — only matches if URL is actually requested)
  • Internal vulnerability scanner enumerating IOC lists from a feed file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sandbox.exe","detonator.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName has "dfir-")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the calling host installed litellm; run `pip show litellm` or query Defender DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory for litellm==1.82.7 or 1.82.8. Pull the full DeviceNetworkEvents window ±5 minutes around the hit to identify the parent Python process and what creds were on disk. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host via MDE Live Response (Isolate-Machine), revoke every credential present on that system (AWS keys, GCP service account JSONs, kubeconfig, .env tokens, SSH keys, npm/Docker tokens) — assume total compromise of the bag, not selective. Rotate via cloud APIs not from the affected host. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to all hosts in the org that installed litellm in the last 14 days via DeviceFileEvents for litellm_init.pth or 'litellm-1.82.7' / 'litellm-1.82.8' in folder paths; for each, run UCs 4-6 against that host range and check K8s audit logs for namespace-wide secret enumeration from in-cluster IPs.

(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

  | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (ExfilDomains) or AdditionalFields has "models.litellm.cloud"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, AdditionalFields, ActionType)
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let ExfilDomains = dynamic(["models.litellm.cloud"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where Name has_any (ExfilDomains) or Name endswith ".litellm.cloud"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName, _ResourceId),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any (ExfilDomains) or RequestURL has "models.litellm.cloud"
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, SourceUserName, ApplicationProtocol),
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (ExfilDomains) or DnsQuery endswith ".litellm.cloud"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseCodeName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious litellm_init.pth dropped to site-packages by pip (litellm==1.82.8 install artifact) AIInstallation High
Detects the install-time artifact unique to litellm 1.82.8 — a 34,628-byte .pth file named litellm_init.pth registered in the package's own RECORD. Because .pth files in site-packages execute on every Python interpreter startup (no import required), this filename appearing anywhere in site-packages is a direct compromise indicator. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim filename 'litellm_init.pth' from the article's RECORD listing (litellm_init.pth,sha256=ceNa7wMJnNHy1kRnNCcwJaFjWX3pORLfMh7xGL8TUjg,34628). The filename is unique to this campaign — no upstream package uses it. Corroborated by Snyk and Datadog Security Labs vendor reports. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/litellm-credential-stealer-hidden-in-pypi-wheel • https://snyk.io/blog/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/compromised-litellm-pypi-package-delivers-multi-stage-credential-stealer
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic capture / mirror of a known-compromised host being copied into an evidence repository (file path will be under /evidence/ or /forensics/)
  • Internal threat-intel lab reproducing the artifact in a controlled VM for analysis
  • Endpoint backup tool snapshotting site-packages contents including a quarantined historical copy
  • Compliance scanner indexing site-packages — generates a read, not a write; UC filters to FileCreated/Modified to avoid this
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\evidence\\" and FolderPath !has "/evidence/" and FolderPath !has "\\forensics\\" and FolderPath !has "/forensics/" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backup-agent","velero")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the FolderPath is a real Python site-packages directory (not /evidence, /backup, /quarantine). Pull `pip show litellm` and check installed version; 1.82.8 is the malicious build. Capture the file SHA256 and compare with the published IOC. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, kill all running Python processes (`pkill -9 python`), uninstall litellm (`pip uninstall -y litellm`), delete the .pth file, and treat all on-host secrets as compromised — rotate SSH keys, cloud credentials, .env values, container registry tokens. Step 3 — Hunt: query DeviceFileEvents for litellm_init.pth across the fleet, then enumerate every CI/CD runner / dev workstation / container image that installed litellm in the last 14 days via package lockfile / SBOM telemetry. Check K8s admission audit for pod images that pinned to 1.82.7 or 1.82.8.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "litellm_init.pth"
   or (FolderPath has "site-packages" and FileName endswith ".pth" and SHA256 == "ceNa7wMJnNHy1kRnNCcwJaFjWX3pORLfMh7xGL8TUjg")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetFileName =~ "litellm_init.pth"
     or (TargetFilePath has "site-packages" and TargetFileName endswith ".pth")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
(Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Facility =~ "auth" or ProcessName has_any ("auditd","audisp")
  | where SyslogMessage has "litellm_init.pth"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python spawning python -c with base64.b64decode exec (litellm .pth stage-1 launcher) AIInstallation High
Detects the exact one-liner the malicious litellm_init.pth file uses to spawn the stage-1 credential harvester — a detached python subprocess that calls base64.b64decode followed by exec(). Pattern fires regardless of payload version because both 1.82.7 (proxy_server.py blob) and 1.82.8 (.pth) decode to the same base64-wrapped Python. Rationale: Anchors on the exact one-liner from the article: subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", "import base64; exec(base64.b64decode('...'))"]). The python→python parent/child with -c + base64.b64decode + exec( triple is unique to obfuscated loaders and is the canonical shape both compromised litellm builds emit. Confirmed across multiple vendor analyses (StepSecurity, Snyk, Datadog Security Labs). Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/litellm-credential-stealer-hidden-in-pypi-wheel • https://snyk.io/blog/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1027 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps tooling that legitimately wraps python startup in obfuscated launchers (e.g., PyArmor-wrapped CLIs, PyInstaller bootstrap scripts)
  • Conda activation script in some niche distributions which uses base64-encoded site-customize hooks
  • Internal CTF or sandboxed malware-analysis VM running known samples
  • ML notebook kernels (Jupyter) that some plugins start via base64-wrapped python -c — verify the parent is jupyter-server
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("jupyter-server","jupyterhub","pyarmor","pyinstaller.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "PyArmor" and ProcessCommandLine !has "pyi-archive_viewer"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: dump the full ProcessCommandLine, base64-decode the blob (limit 50 KB), inspect for keywords from the article (`models.litellm.cloud`, `RSA-4096`, AWS Secrets Manager SDK calls, K8s SA token paths). Confirm parent process is python (not jupyter-server / pyarmor). Step 2 — Contain: kill the child PID immediately, isolate the host, snapshot memory if possible (`gcore` on Linux, MDE live response on Windows) to recover decrypted creds before they hit disk. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to all hosts where a python parent spawned a python -c child in the last 14 days; for any positive, check for the exfil domain (UC1), .pth file (UC2), IMDS hits (UC5), and K8s SA token reads (UC6). Open a vendor ticket if a unique decoded variant differs from published TeamPCP samples — likely a new TeamPCP IOC.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^python\d*(\.exe)?$"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^python\d*(\.exe)?$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-c"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "base64.b64decode"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("exec(","exec (")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\python\d*\.exe$"
  | where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\python\d*\.exe$"
  | where CommandLine has "-c" and CommandLine has "base64.b64decode" and CommandLine has "exec"
  | where AccountName !endswith "$"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, AccountName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)^python\d*(\.exe)?$"
  | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)^python\d*(\.exe)?$"
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-c" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "base64.b64decode" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "exec"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python process spawning shell with TeamPCP recon chain (hostname; whoami; uname; ip addr fallback) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the exact reconnaissance one-liner the litellm stage-1 harvester runs via subprocess.check_output(..., shell=True) before exfiltration. The chained 'hostname; pwd; whoami; uname -a; ip addr 2>/dev/null || ifconfig 2>/dev/null; ip route 2>/dev/null' string is verbatim from the article and rarely emitted by benign tooling. Rationale: The recon command string is byte-for-byte from the article ('hostname; pwd; whoami; uname -a; ip addr 2>/dev/null || ifconfig 2>/dev/null; ip route 2>/dev/null') and is run via shell=True so it shows up as a single child of python with all three discovery primitives in one cmdline. The combination is rare outside config-management tools (Ansible, Chef) which we exclude via parent process. Datadog Security Labs confirmed identical recon string. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/litellm-credential-stealer-hidden-in-pypi-wheel • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/compromised-litellm-pypi-package-delivers-multi-stage-credential-stealer
ATT&CKT1082 T1033 T1016 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible / Salt / Chef facter modules collecting host inventory via python — exclude when parent is /usr/bin/ansible* or salt-minion
  • Datadog or New Relic agent system-info collection at install time
  • Internal sysadmin troubleshooting script that wraps the same recon chain — typically lives in /opt/admin-scripts or runs as root via cron
  • DevOps onboarding bootstrap scripts that probe new VMs (look for parent = cloud-init)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("ansible-playbook","salt-minion","chef-client","puppet","cloud-init","datadog-agent","facter") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/opt/ansible/" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible_facts"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the python parent is not a config-management agent (ansible, salt-minion, puppet, chef-client, cloud-init); validate via parent-of-parent in DeviceProcessEvents. Pull the AccountName — is this a service account that normally runs CI tasks or a human dev session? Step 2 — Contain: snapshot the process tree and command-line history, then isolate the host. If python lineage traces back to a litellm package (check sys.path / pip show via live response), proceed to UC1/UC2 confirmation and treat as full credential compromise. Step 3 — Hunt: search the fleet for the same recon string from python parents (top 50 hosts by AccountName), then pivot to any of those hosts contacting models.litellm.cloud in the same hour window — that pair narrows from 'maybe' to 'confirmed'.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^python\d*(\.exe)?$"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "hostname" and ProcessCommandLine has "whoami" and ProcessCommandLine has "uname")
    or ProcessCommandLine has "ip addr 2>/dev/null || ifconfig"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "hostname" and ProcessCommandLine has "printenv" and ProcessCommandLine has "ip route")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)^python\d*(\.exe)?$"
  | where ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")
  | where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "hostname" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "whoami" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "uname")
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has "ip addr 2>/dev/null || ifconfig"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\python\d*\.exe$"
  | where NewProcessName endswith "cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "pwsh.exe"
  | where (CommandLine has "hostname" and CommandLine has "whoami" and CommandLine has "uname")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
