Python process contacting AWS IMDS 169.254.169.254 (litellm stealer IAM credential theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a Python process reaching out to the AWS Instance Metadata Service at 169.254.169.254 — the exact technique the litellm harvester uses to steal IMDSv2 tokens and exchange them for live IAM role credentials. Combined with parent=python this is high fidelity because the legitimate litellm library has no reason to call IMDS directly. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit IMDS abuse: 'IMDS token + IAM role credentials via 169.254.169.254'. Python connecting to the AWS metadata endpoint is unusual — the boto3 SDK normally only does this when explicitly configured (`AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=false`), and litellm proper has no reason to reach for IAM creds. AWS docs confirm the link-local IP semantics; corroborated by Datadog Security Labs and Snyk. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/litellm-credential-stealer-hidden-in-pypi-wheel • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://snyk.io/blog/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1528
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate boto3-using Python app on EC2 fetching its own role creds at startup (e.g., AWS CLI scripts, custom data-loaders) — exclude per known-good app inventory
  • ECS/EKS init scripts in Python that pull task-role credentials
  • Cloud-init or amazon-ssm-agent helper scripts written in python
  • ML training jobs that fetch S3 creds via IMDS on instance launch — exclude by parent process or container image tag
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "amazon-ssm-agent" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "cfn-init" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ec2-instance-connect" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("cloud-init","systemd")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: from the InitiatingProcessCommandLine, determine the python script being executed; if it's a recognised boto3-using business app, capture process tree (parent + grandparent) and check whether boto3 is the actual caller via memory inspection. Pull CloudTrail for the IAM role within 5 minutes of the IMDS call — look for unusual AccessDenied / GetSecretValue / ListSecrets / DescribeParameters bursts. Step 2 — Contain: revoke the EC2 instance profile session credentials (AWS IAM 'RevokeOlderSessions' on the role), isolate the host, and rotate any long-lived AWS keys present on disk. Step 3 — Hunt: across the AWS org, enumerate every CloudTrail event with userAgent containing 'aws-sdk-python' AND eventName in (ListSecrets, GetSecretValue, DescribeParameters) AND sourceIPAddress matching the affected EC2 instance — these are the post-compromise stolen-creds usage events. Open a session-token audit for the role in question.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^python\d*(\.exe)?$"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(WindowsEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 3 and Provider has "Sysmon"
  | extend Image = tostring(EventData.Image), DestIP = tostring(EventData.DestinationIp), User = tostring(EventData.User), CmdLine = tostring(EventData.CommandLine)
  | where DestIP == "169.254.169.254"
  | where Image matches regex @"(?i)\\python\d*\.exe$" or Image matches regex @"(?i)/python\d*$"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Image, CmdLine, DestIP, User),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254"
  | where SrcUsername has "python" or DvcHostname has ""
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, NetworkProtocol, DstPortNumber)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

In-cluster Kubernetes secret enumeration with Python user-agent (litellm stealer K8s pivot) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the litellm stealer's Kubernetes pivot — after reading /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token from inside a compromised pod, it uses the token to call the K8s API and enumerate Secrets across every namespace. Catches both the on-host token read (endpoint platforms) and the resulting mass secret listing from a python-requests user-agent (K8s audit platforms). Rationale: Anchored on two article-specific signals: (1) the exact filesystem path '/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token' the harvester reads, and (2) the article's statement that the stealer makes 'live API calls to enumerate secrets across all namespaces' — which from a python-requests/urllib3 client leaves a recognisable user-agent in K8s audit. Two complementary telemetry vantage points (endpoint file read + control-plane API call) cover both detection layers. Corroborated by Datadog Security Labs and StepSecurity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/litellm-credential-stealer-hidden-in-pypi-wheel • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/ • https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24518
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528 T1613
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate in-cluster operators / controllers written in Python (kopf, custom CRD operators) that read the SA token to call the K8s API — verify by checking pod labels and known operator image registry
  • Helm hooks / Argo workflow pods that run python jobs needing K8s API access
  • kube-state-metrics or other Prometheus exporters that legitimately list secrets metadata (but not values)
  • Internal devops pods running kubectl-via-python scripts for cluster inventory
Suppression filter
and Subject !startswith "system:serviceaccount:kube-system:" and Subject !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argo:" and Subject !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:" and UserAgent !has "kopf/" and UserAgent !has "prometheus-operator"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the pod and container image emitting the token read / secret enumeration via the K8s audit log Pod identifier; check the image SBOM for litellm 1.82.7 or 1.82.8. Pull the parent ServiceAccount and confirm its RBAC role normally permits cluster-wide secret listing (most app SAs do not). Step 2 — Contain: cordon and drain the affected node; delete the offending Pod (kubectl delete pod --grace-period=0 --force) and disable the bound ServiceAccount (patch RBAC ClusterRoleBindings to remove). Rotate every Secret in every namespace the actor enumerated — assume the secret values were exfiltrated to models.litellm.cloud and treat all downstream creds (DB passwords, registry tokens, OAuth client secrets) as burned. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate every Pod across every cluster whose image contains litellm or whose pip install logs reference 1.82.7/1.82.8 (review build provenance / SBOM telemetry). For each cluster, run the AKSAudit/Kubernetes audit query for the prior 30 day
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath startswith "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount"
   or FileName == "token" and FolderPath has "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^python\d*$"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let MassThreshold = 3;
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where Verb in~ ("list","get","watch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) =~ "secrets"
| extend Subject = tostring(User.username)
| where Subject startswith "system:serviceaccount:"
| where UserAgent has_any ("python-requests","Python/","python-urllib3","urllib3","kubernetes/client-python")
| summarize NamespacesQueried = dcount(tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)),
            SecretsCount = count(),
            Namespaces = make_set(tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), 25),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by Subject, UserAgent, _ResourceId
| where NamespacesQueried >= MassThreshold or SecretsCount >= 20
| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TeamPCP msbuild.exe persistence in user Startup folder · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TeamPCP C2 egress to 83.142.209.203:8080 (telnyx WAV-stego dropper) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TeamPCP tpcp.tar.gz exfil POST signature on egress proxy / WAF · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Telnyx PyPI compromise: malicious telnyx 4.87.1 / 4.87.2 hash on disk AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the two TeamPCP-published malicious telnyx wheels by SHA256 across Defender, Sentinel, and endpoint file telemetry. Pure IOC hit — fires the moment a developer or CI runner installs the backdoored package. Rationale: Both SHA256 hashes are published directly in Aikido's IOC list; matching them is unambiguous. The fallback path-match on telnyx/_client.py catches the case where pip extracts the wheel and the hash hits the cache before EDR scans the wheel itself. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/telnyx-pypi-compromised-teampcp-canisterworm
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally retains malicious sample for analysis in sandbox VM
  • Defender quarantine path itself flagged after first detection
  • Vendor IOC scanner downloads the hash for signature testing
  • Backup snapshot of compromised dev workstation restored to clean host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the host's pip log (~/.pip/pip.log or %APPDATA%\pip\pip.log) and confirm the malicious version was installed; identify the requirements.txt / poetry.lock / lockfile that pulled it. Contain: isolate the host, rotate every credential reachable from that environment (cloud keys, GitHub PATs, npm/PyPI tokens, SSH keys, .env contents) — assume full exfil. Hunt: check all peer dev hosts and CI runners for the same hashes, audit pinning policy across requirements files, and search outbound connection logs to 83.142.209.203 for the past 14 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in ("7321caa303fe96ded0492c747d2f353c4f7d17185656fe292ab0a59e2bd0b8d9","cd08115806662469bbedec4b03f8427b97c8a4b3bc1442dc18b72b4e19395fe3")
   or (FolderPath has @"\telnyx\" and FileName =~ "_client.py")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileOriginUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in ("7321caa303fe96ded0492c747d2f353c4f7d17185656fe292ab0a59e2bd0b8d9","cd08115806662469bbedec4b03f8427b97c8a4b3bc1442dc18b72b4e19395fe3")
   or (TargetFilePath has @"\telnyx\" and TargetFileName =~ "_client.py")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256

TeamPCP C2 egress to 83.142.209.203:8080 (telnyx WAV-stego dropper) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any host-initiated TCP connection to TeamPCP's hard-coded C2 IP on port 8080. This is where both the Windows hangup.wav and Linux/Mac ringtone.wav payloads are fetched from and where AES-encrypted tpcp.tar.gz bundles are POSTed back. Rationale: 83.142.209.203 is the sole C2 IP listed in Aikido's IOC block and serves both the Windows and Linux dropper as well as the exfil channel. Any outbound to this address from a non-sandbox host is a high-fidelity supply-chain compromise indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/telnyx-pypi-compromised-teampcp-canisterworm
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox legitimately fetching the sample for analysis
  • Aikido / Snyk / Socket scanner IP-reputation probe from a known scanner host
  • SOC dropper-replay test on isolated lab subnet
  • VPN egress NAT shared with another organisation that triggered first
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("AikidoScanner.exe", "socket-cli.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: identify the initiating process (python.exe, pip.exe, an installed app importing telnyx) and confirm whether telnyx 4.87.1/4.87.2 is present on the host or in pip cache. Contain: block 83.142.209.203 at the egress firewall/proxy, isolate the host, kill the initiating process tree. Hunt: pivot to DeviceFileEvents for hangup.wav / ringtone.wav writes on the same host, then look for msbuild.exe in the Startup folder; rotate every secret reachable from the compromised environment.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "83.142.209.203"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationIP == "83.142.209.203" or RequestURL has "83.142.209.203"
   | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceAction),
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstIpAddr == "83.142.209.203"
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction, Url)

TeamPCP WAV-stego payload drop (hangup.wav / ringtone.wav) AIDelivery High
Detects creation of hangup.wav or ringtone.wav files on disk that were sourced from C2 IP 83.142.209.203, the WAV-steganography carriers TeamPCP uses to deliver the second-stage executable (Windows) or Python script (Linux/Mac). Joins file-create telemetry to the network origin URL so a benign hangup.wav from a SIP client doesn't fire. Rationale: Aikido names the two specific filenames (hangup.wav, ringtone.wav) served from 83.142.209.203:8080. Correlating the filename with the C2-IP origin or a near-simultaneous network connect from the same host eliminates the FP risk of legitimate SIP/UC apps writing similarly-named ringtone assets. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/telnyx-pypi-compromised-teampcp-canisterworm
ATT&CKT1027.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VoIP / softphone client (Telnyx desktop app itself, Zoiper, MicroSIP) installing or updating audio asset bundles
  • Audio editor scratch files happening to be named hangup.wav
  • End-user downloading a ringtone from a generic ringtone site
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample on a security analyst's workstation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("telnyx.exe","zoiper.exe","microsip.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: confirm FileOriginUrl / FileOriginIP equals 83.142.209.203 — if so, treat as confirmed. Pull the parent process; it will typically be python.exe with telnyx in the command line. Contain: kill the python process tree, isolate the host, remove the WAV file and any %APPDATA%\...\Startup\msbuild.exe drop. Hunt: search the broader fleet for the same filename + C2 IP combo; look for any developer / CI host that imported telnyx in the past 7 days.
let WavDrop = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("hangup.wav","ringtone.wav")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, SHA256;
let C2Hosts = DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteIP == "83.142.209.203"
  | distinct DeviceId;
WavDrop
| where FileOriginIP == "83.142.209.203" or FileOriginUrl has "83.142.209.203" or DeviceId in (C2Hosts)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("hangup.wav","ringtone.wav")
| join kind=inner (
    ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr == "83.142.209.203"
    | project DvcHostname, ConnTime = TimeGenerated
  ) on DvcHostname
| where abs(datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, ConnTime)) <= 5
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ConnTime

#event_simpleName=FileWritten | (TargetFileName=/\\hangup\.wav$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\ringtone\.wav$/i OR TargetFileName=/\/hangup\.wav$/i OR TargetFileName=/\/ringtone\.wav$/i) | join({#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 | RemoteAddressIP4="83.142.209.203"}, field=aid)

TeamPCP msbuild.exe persistence in user Startup folder AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a file named msbuild.exe under the per-user Startup folder %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup, the renamed-binary persistence TeamPCP uses on Windows. Legitimate msbuild.exe lives under Program Files, never in Startup, making the path the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: The Aikido article explicitly names %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\msbuild.exe and its .lock companion as the persistence artefacts. Genuine msbuild.exe never lives in a user's Startup folder, so the path itself is the discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/telnyx-pypi-compromised-teampcp-canisterworm
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT pushing a custom shortcut bundle that happens to use the msbuild name (extremely rare)
  • Developer manually copying a build helper named msbuild.exe to Startup for testing
  • Group Policy startup-script writing a benign helper with the same name
  • Sandbox detonation by the SOC team itself
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\"
Response runbook
Triage: verify SHA256 of the dropped file — if it does not match the legitimate Microsoft MSBuild signing chain (signer = Microsoft Corporation), treat as confirmed malicious. Contain: isolate host, delete msbuild.exe + msbuild.exe.lock from Startup folder, kill any running instance, rotate credentials cached on that workstation. Hunt: pivot back to which python.exe + telnyx import dropped it (DeviceFileEvents InitiatingProcess columns), then sweep the fleet for the same filename-in-Startup pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("msbuild.exe","msbuild.exe.lock")
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("msbuild.exe","msbuild.exe.lock")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256

TeamPCP Linux/Mac stdin-piped Python second stage (sys.executable -) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the Linux/macOS branch of the telnyx backdoor: _client.py base64-decodes a script and runs it via sys.executable with '-' as the argument, piping the third-stage collector to stdin. The 'python3 -' or 'python -' invocation with no script file from a non-interactive parent is the article-specific behavioural signature. Rationale: Article states the Linux/Mac branch 'runs it via sys.executable - piped to stdin' from the base64 blob at telnyx/_client.py line 459. python being its own parent and being invoked with a bare '-' is a very rare shape; combined with a same-host hit on the named C2 it becomes high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/telnyx-pypi-compromised-teampcp-canisterworm
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD job using 'python -' pattern to feed a heredoc script (Jenkins, GitLab runners)
  • Ansible / SaltStack module that pipes a python module body to a remote interpreter
  • Developer running 'cat foo.py | python -' for debugging
  • Docker build step using python with stdin to bootstrap a tool
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/builds/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/github/workspace/"
Response runbook
Triage: read the full command line and parent context — if same-host saw outbound to 83.142.209.203 within 15 minutes, confirmed. Inspect /proc/<pid>/cmdline and lsof for the stdin-fed script if process still running; capture memory if possible. Contain: kill the process tree, quarantine any ringtone.wav cached under /tmp or the user home, isolate the host, rotate every credential the user account can reach. Hunt: enumerate every host that has telnyx 4.87.1/4.87.2 installed via pip show / pip freeze inventory; sweep DNS/proxy for ringtone.wav HTTP downloads.
let PyExecDash = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName matches regex @"^python[0-9.]*$"
  | where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bpython[0-9.]*\s+-\s*$"
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^python[0-9.]*$"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath;
let C2Hit = DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteIP == "83.142.209.203"
  | summarize ConnTime = min(Timestamp) by DeviceName;
PyExecDash
| join kind=inner C2Hit on DeviceName
| where abs(datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ConnTime)) <= 15
| order by Timestamp desc
let PyExecDash = ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)^python[0-9.]*$"
  | where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bpython[0-9.]*\s+-\s*$"
  | where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)^python[0-9.]*$"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine;
let C2Hit = ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr == "83.142.209.203"
  | summarize ConnTime = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname;
PyExecDash
| join kind=inner C2Hit on DvcHostname
| where abs(datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, ConnTime)) <= 15
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*"python3 -"* OR *"python -"*) @process.parent.name:(python OR python3 OR python3.11 OR python3.12)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ImageFileName=/\/python[0-9.]*$/i | CommandLine=/\bpython[0-9.]*\s+-\s*$/i | ParentBaseFileName=/^python[0-9.]*$/i | join({#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 | RemoteAddressIP4="83.142.209.203"}, field=aid) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_cmd values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="python" OR Processes.process_name="python3" OR Processes.process_name="python3.11" OR Processes.process_name="python3.12") AND Processes.process IN ("*python3 -","*python -","*python3.* -") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","python3.11","python3.12") by host Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join host [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="83.142.209.203" by host | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | rename count as c2_hits | fields host c2_hits] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
TeamPCP tpcp.tar.gz exfil POST signature on egress proxy / WAF AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exfiltration leg of the telnyx backdoor: an HTTP POST to 83.142.209.203:8080 carrying the X-Filename: tpcp.tar.gz header or a body referencing the same filename. Proxy / WAF / CommonSecurityLog telemetry catches the egress even when the host EDR did not see the WAV drop (e.g. unmanaged dev laptop on corp network). Rationale: Aikido explicitly names the exfil header X-Filename: tpcp.tar.gz, destination 83.142.209.203:8080, and POST method. Three independent IOCs in one query make this near-zero FP; the WAF/proxy variant catches even unmanaged endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/telnyx-pypi-compromised-teampcp-canisterworm
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-hunter intentionally generating exfil traffic for a tabletop
  • Aikido / Snyk telemetry endpoint sharing the IP (verify ownership before allowlisting)
  • Backup tool happening to upload a file literally named tpcp.tar.gz (extremely unlikely)
  • Penetration-test team mimicking TeamPCP TTPs during a red-team engagement
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("redteam","pentest")
Response runbook
Triage: confirm POST + 83.142.209.203:8080 + tpcp.tar.gz reference; this combination is intentional and IOC-grade. Identify the source host and user account. Contain: block the C2 IP at the perimeter, isolate the source host, pull the python process tree, preserve memory if reachable, treat ALL credentials reachable from that environment as compromised (cloud, GitHub, npm, PyPI, SSH, .env, AWS Bedrock / OpenAI / Anthropic API keys). Hunt: pivot to telnyx-installed inventory across the fleet; check egress for any past connection to the C2 over the previous 14 days even without the tpcp.tar.gz marker, since session was successful only on the leg that included exfil.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "83.142.209.203" and RemotePort == 8080
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "tpcp.tar.gz"
    | project DeviceName, ExfilTime = Timestamp, FolderPath, FileName
  ) on DeviceName
| where isnotempty(ExfilTime) or InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^python[0-9.]*(\.exe)?$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ExfilTime, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationIP == "83.142.209.203" or RequestURL has "83.142.209.203"
   | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
   | where FileName =~ "tpcp.tar.gz" or RequestURL has "tpcp.tar.gz" or Message has "tpcp.tar.gz"
   | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, FileName, Message, DeviceAction),
  (ImWebSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstIpAddr == "83.142.209.203" or Url has "83.142.209.203"
   | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
   | where FileName =~ "tpcp.tar.gz" or Url has "tpcp.tar.gz"
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, HttpMethod, Url, FileName, ThreatName, DvcAction)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33634")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7321caa303fe96ded0492c747d2f353c4f7d17185656fe292ab0a59e2bd0b8d9", "cd08115806662469bbedec4b03f8427b97c8a4b3bc1442dc18b72b4e19395fe3") or SHA1 in~ ("7321caa303fe96ded0492c747d2f353c4f7d17185656fe292ab0a59e2bd0b8d9", "cd08115806662469bbedec4b03f8427b97c8a4b3bc1442dc18b72b4e19395fe3") or MD5 in~ ("7321caa303fe96ded0492c747d2f353c4f7d17185656fe292ab0a59e2bd0b8d9", "cd08115806662469bbedec4b03f8427b97c8a4b3bc1442dc18b72b4e19395fe3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7321caa303fe96ded0492c747d2f353c4f7d17185656fe292ab0a59e2bd0b8d9", "cd08115806662469bbedec4b03f8427b97c8a4b3bc1442dc18b72b4e19395fe3") or SHA1 in~ ("7321caa303fe96ded0492c747d2f353c4f7d17185656fe292ab0a59e2bd0b8d9", "cd08115806662469bbedec4b03f8427b97c8a4b3bc1442dc18b72b4e19395fe3") or MD5 in~ ("7321caa303fe96ded0492c747d2f353c4f7d17185656fe292ab0a59e2bd0b8d9", "cd08115806662469bbedec4b03f8427b97c8a4b3bc1442dc18b72b4e19395fe3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7321caa303fe96ded0492c747d2f353c4f7d17185656fe292ab0a59e2bd0b8d9", "cd08115806662469bbedec4b03f8427b97c8a4b3bc1442dc18b72b4e19395fe3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Silver Fox Japan tax-season lure: inbound email with Japanese HR/ESOP subject + gofile.io URL or RAR/ZIP AIDelivery High
Hunts the specific Silver Fox tax-season campaign against Japanese firms by joining inbound email with Japanese tax/HR/ESOP keyword subjects to either a gofile.io download URL or a RAR/ZIP attachment. Article explicitly names these subject patterns and gofile.io as the file hosting abused. Rationale: Subject fragments are pulled verbatim from the article's listed lures; gofile.io and WeTransfer are the hosting services the article explicitly calls out as red flags. Cross-checked with Sekoia's 'Silver Fox: only tax audit where the fine print installs malware' analysis and Hacker News' Oct-2025 Japan/Malaysia coverage which confirm the same lure shape and archive-based delivery for this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/silver-fox-the-only-tax-audit-where-the-fine-print-installs-malware/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/silver-fox-expands-winos-40-attacks-to.html • https://www.rescana.com/post/silver-fox-expands-winos-4-0-valleyrat-and-holdinghands-rat-cyber-attacks-to-japan-and-malaysia
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1566.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let JpLureSubjectFragments = dynamic(["従業員持株会","人事異動","給与改定","給与調整","税務コンプライアンス","罰金通知","持株会規約"]);
let ArchiveTypes = dynamic(["rar","zip","RAR","ZIP","7z","7Z"]);
let SuspectMail = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
    | where Subject contains "従業員持株会"
        or Subject contains "人事異動"
        or Subject contains "給与改定"
        or Subject contains "給与調整"
        or Subject contains "税務コンプライアンス"
        or Subject contains "罰金通知"
        or Subject contains "持株会規約"
    | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AuthenticationDetails;
let UrlSide = SuspectMail
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailUrlInfo
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where UrlDomain has_any ("gofile.io","wetransfer.com","we.tl")
        | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | extend Vector = strcat("URL:", UrlDomain), Indicator = Url;
let AttachSide = SuspectMail
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailAttachmentInfo
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where FileType in~ (ArchiveTypes) or FileName endswith ".rar" or FileName endswith ".zip" or FileName endswith ".7z"
        | project NetworkMessageId, FileName, FileType, SHA256, FileSize
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | extend Vector = strcat("ATTACH:", FileType), Indicator = FileName;
union UrlSide, AttachSide
| project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, Subject, Vector, Indicator, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
OfficeActivity

| where Subject contains "従業員持株会"

| order by TimeGenerated desc
gofile.io archive download by browser followed by extracted-EXE execution within 30 minutes AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a file pulled from gofile.io by a browser/Outlook to a subsequent unsigned-or-temp-path executable launch on the same host within 30 minutes. Article calls out gofile.io as Silver Fox's chosen drop site and notes the payload is delivered inside RAR/ZIP archives, so this catches the post-click stage even when the email itself slipped past the gateway. Rationale: Article explicitly names gofile.io and WeTransfer as the hosting services Silver Fox abuses for the Japan tax-season campaign, plus calls out RAR/ZIP archives as the carrier. The 30-minute correlation window + extraction-tool parent set turns the broad 'file from gofile.io' signal into a high-fidelity post-extraction execution alert. Cross-checked Dark Lab and Sekoia ValleyRAT campaign write-ups which confirm the gofile.io / archive pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.darklab.hk/2026/03/25/silver-foxs-dual-pronged-strategy-dissecting-the-valleyrat-distribution-campaign/ • https://blog.sekoia.io/silver-fox-the-only-tax-audit-where-the-fine-print-installs-malware/

| where TimeGenerated between (DownloadTime .. DownloadTime + WindowMin)
| project TimeGenerated, DownloadTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, DownloadTime), DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Url, FileName_dl, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ValleyRAT registry-resident shellcode (HKCU\Console\0|1) and MyPythonApp Run-key persistence AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ValleyRAT family persistence and shellcode-storage artefacts that Silver Fox deploys after initial execution: a value named d33f351a4aeea5e608853d1a56661059 written into HKCU\Console\0 or HKCU\Console\1 (encrypted shellcode store), and the MyPythonApp Run-key persistence value. Single-event detection — high signal because both names are unique to ValleyRAT. Rationale: Article confirms ValleyRAT (Win64/Valley) is the payload Silver Fox drops in this Japan tax-season campaign. The two registry indicators - HKCU\Console\{0,1} value d33f351a4aeea5e608853d1a56661059 and Run-key value MyPythonApp - are family-level ValleyRAT artefacts documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz and Fortinet FortiGuard, so a hit means a ValleyRAT install regardless of which Silver Fox sub-campaign delivered it. Cross-checked against: • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/technical-analysis-latest-variant-valleyrat • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/valleyrat-campaign-targeting-chinese-speakers • https://any.run/malware-trends/valleyrat/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1112 T1027.013

DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where (RegistryKey has_cs @"\Console\0" or RegistryKey has_cs @"\Console\1") and RegistryValueName =~ "d33f351a4aeea5e608853d1a56661059"
    or (RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" and RegistryValueName =~ "MyPythonApp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueType, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where (RegistryKey has_cs @"\Console\0" or RegistryKey has_cs @"\Console\1") and RegistryValue =~ "d33f351a4aeea5e608853d1a56661059"
    or (RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" and RegistryValue =~ "MyPythonApp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueType, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TeamPCP supply-chain C2 — outbound to checkmarx[.]zone / 83.142.209.11 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts CI/CD runner hosts (and any endpoint) connecting to the TeamPCP exfiltration domain checkmarx[.]zone or its hosting IP 83.142.209[.]11, used to receive AES-256-CBC encrypted tpcp.tar.gz archives from compromised Checkmarx/kics-github-action setup.sh runs between 12:58–16:50 UTC on 2026-03-23. Same infrastructure family as the Trivy compromise — actor reuses domain. Rationale: checkmarx[.]zone and 83.142.209.11 are attacker-controlled typosquat exfil infrastructure confirmed by Wiz, Unit 42 and StepSecurity. checkmarx.zone has no legitimate use — any connection to it is high-confidence compromise. Article + Wiz blog cited for IP and domain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/teampcp-attack-kics-github-action • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/teampcp-hacks-checkmarx-github-actions.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/24/detecting-investigating-defending-against-trivy-supply-chain-compromise/

TeamPCP systemd backdoor — sysmon.py / sysmon.service persistence on CI runner AIInstallation High
Hunts the file-system fingerprint of the TeamPCP persistence stage: a python implant dropped at ~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py (or /root/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py in K8s pods) and a user-mode systemd unit at ~/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service that polls https://checkmarx[.]zone/raw every 3000 seconds. Both paths are unique to TeamPCP and recur across the Trivy and KICS compromises. Rationale: The path tuple ~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py + ~/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service is unique to TeamPCP and is documented by Wiz as the persistence mechanism in both the KICS and Trivy compromises. No legitimate Linux software writes both paths. The article references systemd persistence; Wiz provided the exact filenames. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/teampcp-attack-kics-github-action • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/from-scanner-to-stealer-inside-the-trivy-action-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1195.002 T1059.006

    or ( FolderPath has "/.config/systemd/user" and FileName =~ "sysmon.service" )
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where ( TargetFilePath has "/.config/sysmon" and TargetFileName =~ "sysmon.py" )
    or ( TargetFilePath has "/.config/systemd/user" and TargetFileName =~ "sysmon.service" )
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSize,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TeamPCP exfiltration archive — tpcp.tar.gz file creation on host AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the AES-256-CBC encrypted exfiltration archive tpcp.tar.gz produced by the compromised setup.sh after harvesting AWS/Azure/GCP credentials, SSH keys, Kubernetes service-account tokens and Runner.Worker memory contents. Same archive name reused in the prior Trivy supply-chain compromise — the static filename is the actor's tradecraft signature. Rationale: tpcp.tar.gz is the literal exfil filename documented by Wiz for both the Trivy and KICS compromises — actor tradecraft signature, not a generic name. The article references the encrypted exfil to checkmarx.zone; Wiz blog supplied the archive filename and the AES-256-CBC mechanism. Pairing a 30-day lookback catches stragglers from compromised pipelines that ran during the 12:58–16:50 UTC window on 2026-03-23. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/teampcp-attack-kics-github-action • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/teampcp-hacks-checkmarx-github-actions.html

          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessParentCreationTime
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "tpcp.tar.gz"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CanisterWorm: How a Self-Propagating npm Worm Is Spreading Backdoors Across the Ecosystem

StepSecurity
2026-03-26 7 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Following Trivy's compromise, StepSecurity's AI Package Analyst flagged suspicious new releases across multiple npm scopes — revealing CanisterWorm, a self-propagating npm worm deployed by the TeamPCP threat actor. The worm is a direct continuation of the second Trivy compromise (v0.69.4): attackers embedded a credential harvester in Trivy's CI/CD toolchain, stole npm tokens from affected pipelines, then used those tokens to publish backdoored patch versions across every namespace they could reach — including the @opengov scope (16+ packages).

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
