Trivy Compromised a Second Time - Malicious v0.69.4 Release, aquasecurity/setup-trivy, aquasecurity/trivy-action GitHub Actions Compromised

StepSecurity
2026-03-26 10 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On March 19, 2026, trivy — a widely used open source vulnerability scanner maintained by Aqua Security — experienced a second security incident. Three weeks after the hackerbot-claw incident on February 28 that resulted in a repository takeover, a new compromised release (v0.69.4) was published to the trivy repository. The original incident disclosure discussion (#10265) was also deleted during this period, and version tags on the aquasecurity/setup-trivy GitHub Action were removed. Trivy maintainers deleted the v0.69.4 tag and Homebrew downgraded to v0.69.3. The following is a factual account…

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Trivy Compromised a Second Time - Malicious v0.69.4 Release, aquasecurity/setup-
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Compromised trivy binary (v0.69.4-v0.69.6) execution by SHA1 hash · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Trivy supply-chain C2 beacon to typosquat domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GitHub Actions runner credential stealer: python3 base64-decoded payload reading /proc/<pid>/mem · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Trivy supply-chain C2 beacon to typosquat domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org AICommand & Control High
Hunts any DNS resolution, web request, or outbound socket targeting the attacker-controlled typosquat domain scan.aquasecurtiy.org (note the misspelled 'aquasecurtiy'). This domain received RSA-encrypted GitHub Actions runner secrets harvested by the compromised aquasecurity/trivy-action, aquasecurity/setup-trivy, and trivy v0.69.4-0.69.6 binaries during the March 2026 supply-chain incident. Rationale: The typosquat domain 'aquasecurtiy.org' (misspelled — extra 't' before 'iy') is the single exfiltration channel for every variant of this compromise (trivy-action entrypoint.sh, setup-trivy action.yaml commit 8afa9b9, and trivy v0.69.4-0.69.6 hardcoded). The misspelling is unique enough that any hit anywhere in the estate is a confirmed compromise — independently verified by Aqua Security GHSA, The Hacker News, Snyk and Palo Alto Networks write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/trivy-security-scanner-github-actions.html • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/trivy-supply-chain-attack-what-you-need-to-know/ • https://snyk.io/articles/trivy-github-actions-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/blog/cloud-security/trivy-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567 T1583.001

Compromised trivy binary (v0.69.4-v0.69.6) execution by SHA1 hash AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the malicious trivy binaries released during the March 2026 ecosystem compromise. SHA1 hashes were recovered from the deleted incident discussion #10265 and Docker Hub images aquasec/trivy:0.69.5 and 0.69.6. Any execution of these hashes confirms a compromised CI runner or developer workstation that downloaded trivy during the ~3-hour window. Rationale: Eight SHA1 hashes pre-extracted from the article correspond to the malicious trivy binaries (v0.69.4 GitHub Release + Docker images aquasec/trivy:0.69.5 / 0.69.6) plus modified entrypoint.sh / action.yaml artifacts. Aqua Security advisory GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 and the Snyk write-up confirm these are the campaign's primary delivery artefacts. Hash match has near-zero FP — only legitimate clean builds re-publishing the same fingerprint could ever collide. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/trivy-supply-chain-attack-what-you-need-to-know/ • https://snyk.io/articles/trivy-github-actions-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059

GitHub Actions runner credential stealer: python3 base64-decoded payload reading /proc/<pid>/mem AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-stealer execution pattern injected into entrypoint.sh (trivy-action) and action.yaml (setup-trivy@8afa9b9) — bash decodes a base64 Python blob which then opens /proc/<Runner.Worker pid>/mem to extract GitHub Actions secrets marked isSecret:true. Targets Linux self-hosted runners and developer workstations where the action ran outside hosted runner ephemera. Rationale: The article explicitly documents the credential-stealer chain: entrypoint.sh / action.yaml bash decodes a base64 Python blob; the python3 child opens /proc/<Runner.Worker pid>/mem to dump GitHub Actions secrets (StepSecurity Harden-Runner labelled this exact pattern 'Runner Worker Memory Read', PID 2538 → /proc/2167/mem in their controlled replay). The combination of python3-child-of-bash + base64 decode + /proc/<pid>/mem access from a runner working directory is article-specific and not covered by generic LOLBin or LSASS-access rules. Skipped Sigma because the detection requires multi-condition correlation (parent cmdline + child cmdline + path context) rather than a single-event selection block. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 • https://www.upwind.io/feed/trivy-supply-chain-incident-github-actions-compromise-breakdown • https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/blog/cloud-security/trivy-supply-chain-attack/ • https://mrcloudbook.com/how-trivy-was-compromised-to-deliver-malware-again/
ATT&CKT1003 T1552.001 T1027.013 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python3","python")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","Runner.Worker","node","entrypoint.sh")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64","b64decode","/proc/","Runner.Worker","isSecret")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64 -d","base64 --decode","entrypoint.sh","aquasecurity","trivy")
| extend mem_read = iff(ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/\d+/mem", "yes", "")
| extend b64_pipe = iff(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "base64" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "python", "yes", "")
| extend ci_context = iff(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("entrypoint.sh","aquasecurity","trivy","GITHUB_ACTIONS","RUNNER_") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/runner/","/_work/","/_actions/","/home/runner/"), "yes", "")
| where mem_read == "yes" or b64_pipe == "yes" or ci_context == "yes"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          mem_read, b64_pipe, ci_context
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

   or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64 -d","base64 --decode","entrypoint.sh","aquasecurity","trivy")

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 Compromised on PyPI - Backdoor Exfiltrates Private Keys

StepSecurity
2026-03-26 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On March 17, 2026, bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 was identified as a compromised PyPI package. The malicious release had been live on PyPI for approximately 48 hours before being yanked. This post is a ground-up technical breakdown based on a direct diff of the source tarballs for versions 4.0.1 and 4.0.2 — covering exactly what changed, how the backdoor works, and what defenders should do. We also ran the compromised package with StepSecurity Harden Runner and captured every C2 channel firing in real time.

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 source-tarball SHA256 on disk
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 Compromised on PyPI - Backdoor Exfiltrates Private Keys
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 backdoor C2 domain contact (opentensor-* lookalikes) · [LLM] DNS tunneling exfiltration pattern to *.t.opentensor-cdn.com (hex chunk/index/total/session) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 backdoor C2 domain contact (opentensor-* lookalikes) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS lookups and outbound connections to the four hard-coded / parent-zone C2 domains used by the bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 PyPI backdoor (opentensor-metrics.com, subtensor-telemetry.com, metagraph-stats.com, opentensor-cdn.com). These domains impersonate legitimate Bittensor infrastructure (opentensor.ai, subtensor, metagraph) and are contacted from python3.12 within ~2 seconds of any coldkey/hotkey decryption. Rationale: All four domains are explicitly named in the article as attacker-controlled lookalike infrastructure confirmed contacted by python3.12 during Harden Runner instrumentation; opentensor-cdn.com is the parent zone for both the DGA rotation (*.opentensor-cdn.com) and the DNS-tunnel egress (t.opentensor-cdn.com), so the suffix match covers all three C2 layers in one rule. No legitimate Bittensor service resolves under these squat zones. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/bittensor-wallet-4-0-2-compromised-on-pypi---backdoor-exfiltrates-private-keys
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1568.002 T1195.002

  | where (isnotempty(DstHostname) and DstHostname has_any (_c2_domains)) or (isnotempty(Url) and Url has_any (_c2_domains))
  | extend Indicator = coalesce(DstHostname, Url)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, EvtSource="ImNet", Indicator),
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Name has_any (_c2_domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=Computer, SrcIpAddr=ClientIP, EvtSource="DnsEvents", Indicator=Name)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS tunneling exfiltration pattern to *.t.opentensor-cdn.com (hex chunk/index/total/session) AICommand & Control High
Detects the chunked DNS-A exfiltration channel used by the bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 backdoor when its HTTPS C2 attempts fail. Each NaCl-sealed private-key payload is hex-encoded, split into 60-char chunks, and emitted as A queries shaped <hex>.<index>.<total>.<session_id>.t.opentensor-cdn.com. The regex shape is highly specific and a single match constitutes confirmed exfiltration. Rationale: The article shows 28 real chunks captured by Harden Runner with the exact <hex>.<idx>.<total>.<session>.t.opentensor-cdn.com label shape (session 52016, total 28). The regex matches that schema and only that schema, so a single query is enough to alert; the >=3 chunk threshold in SPL/KQL is purely a noise-floor sanity guard. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/bittensor-wallet-4-0-2-compromised-on-pypi---backdoor-exfiltrates-private-keys
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| extend QueryName = tolower(tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).QueryName))
| where QueryName endswith ".t.opentensor-cdn.com"
| where QueryName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{40,}\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.t\.opentensor-cdn\.com$"
| extend SessionId = extract(@"\.([0-9]+)\.t\.opentensor-cdn\.com$", 1, QueryName)
| extend ChunkTotal = extract(@"\.([0-9]+)\.[0-9]+\.t\.opentensor-cdn\.com$", 1, QueryName)
| summarize ChunkCount = count(),
            Sessions = make_set(SessionId, 10),
            ExpectedTotal = make_set(ChunkTotal, 5),
            SampleQueries = make_set(QueryName, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen  = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where ChunkCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DnsQuery endswith ".t.opentensor-cdn.com"
  | where DnsQuery matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{40,}\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.t\.opentensor-cdn\.com$"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery),
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Name endswith ".t.opentensor-cdn.com"
  | where Name matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{40,}\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.t\.opentensor-cdn\.com$"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=Computer, SrcIpAddr=ClientIP, DnsQuery=Name)
| extend SessionId = extract(@"\.([0-9]+)\.t\.opentensor-cdn\.com$", 1, DnsQuery)
| extend ChunkTotal = extract(@"\.([0-9]+)\.[0-9]+\.t\.opentensor-cdn\.com$", 1, DnsQuery)
| summarize ChunkCount = count(),
            Sessions = make_set(SessionId, 10),
            ExpectedTotal = make_set(ChunkTotal, 5),
            SampleQueries = make_set(DnsQuery, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen  = max(TimeGenerated)
            by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr
| where ChunkCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc

Compromised bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 source-tarball SHA256 on disk AIDelivery Medium
Identifies any host (developer workstation, CI runner, validator/miner box) that has the malicious bittensor-wallet 4.0.2 source tarball or its derived wheel artifacts on disk. Presence of either hash means the backdoored package was downloaded and almost certainly built/installed; any wallet decryption performed while it was active should be treated as a confirmed coldkey/hotkey compromise. Rationale: Both SHA256 values are the pre-extracted IOCs from the StepSecurity post for the malicious 4.0.2 source tarball (primary) and its derived artifact (secondary). Hash equality on a file or process event is a definitive supply-chain compromise indicator with effectively zero false-positive risk. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/bittensor-wallet-4-0-2-compromised-on-pypi---backdoor-exfiltrates-private-keys
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
let _bad_hashes = dynamic([
  "6a416b72ff24804abc12484a3b41413a8580acedd8a5f8c84224fcf0732c2f8e",
  "edc2588d5e272835285e4171dd3daf862149f617015bf52e43d433d8e5c297c5"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA256 in (_bad_hashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA256 in (_bad_hashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (_bad_hashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessEvent", ActionType="ProcessCreated", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let _bad_hashes = dynamic([
  "6a416b72ff24804abc12484a3b41413a8580acedd8a5f8c84224fcf0732c2f8e",
  "edc2588d5e272835285e4171dd3daf862149f617015bf52e43d433d8e5c297c5"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in (_bad_hashes) or Hash in (_bad_hashes)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a416b72ff24804abc12484a3b41413a8580acedd8a5f8c84224fcf0732c2f8e") or SHA1 in~ ("6a416b72ff24804abc12484a3b41413a8580acedd8a5f8c84224fcf0732c2f8e") or MD5 in~ ("6a416b72ff24804abc12484a3b41413a8580acedd8a5f8c84224fcf0732c2f8e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a416b72ff24804abc12484a3b41413a8580acedd8a5f8c84224fcf0732c2f8e") or SHA1 in~ ("6a416b72ff24804abc12484a3b41413a8580acedd8a5f8c84224fcf0732c2f8e") or MD5 in~ ("6a416b72ff24804abc12484a3b41413a8580acedd8a5f8c84224fcf0732c2f8e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6a416b72ff24804abc12484a3b41413a8580acedd8a5f8c84224fcf0732c2f8e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious npm Releases Found in Popular React Native Packages - 130K+ Monthly Downloads Compromised

StepSecurity
2026-03-26 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On March 16, 2026, StepSecurity Threat Intel was the first to detect and report malicious releases in two popular React Native npm packages — react-native-international-phone-number and react-native-country-select. StepSecurity's AI Package Analyst flagged the compromised versions, and within minutes, StepSecurity filed security issues directly in both GitHub repositories — alerting the maintainer and the community before any other security vendor.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised react-native-international-phone-number / react-native-country-select files written to node_modules · [LLM] Attacker-controlled scoped npm relay packages on disk (@usebioerhold8733 / @agnoliaarisian7180)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Malicious npm Releases Found in Popular React Native Packages - 130K+ Monthly Do
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm postinstall hook spawning node init.js or child.js (React Native attack pattern)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] node.exe contacting Solana JSON-RPC endpoints (suspected blockchain dead-drop C2) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Compromised react-native-international-phone-number / react-native-country-select files written to node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Hunts hosts where the two known-compromised React Native npm packages have been installed into a node_modules tree. Article-specific because it targets the two named packages from the StepSecurity disclosure rather than generic npm telemetry; presence alone warrants a developer-workstation review since @latest currently resolves to compromised versions. Rationale: Anchors on the two named compromised npm packages from the article. File-system writes inside node_modules/<pkg>/ confirm the dep is present on a host regardless of which lockfile pinned it; analyst then opens the package.json to confirm the version is one of the listed bad ones (0.11.8 / 0.12.1-3 / 0.3.91 / 0.4.1-2).
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer who pinned the last-known-safe versions (0.11.7 / 0.4.0) and re-ran yarn/npm install
  • CI build agent restoring node_modules cache for a project that uses these packages
  • Mobile dev pulling main branch and re-running install with safe-pinned versions
  • Security researcher running this article's IOCs on a sandbox host
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\node_modules\\react-native-international-phone-number\\package.json","\\node_modules\\react-native-country-select\\package.json") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("0.11.7","0.4.0"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): On the affected host, open the package.json sibling to the written files and check the version field; confirm whether it matches the published-bad list (0.11.8, 0.12.1-3 for international-phone-number; 0.3.91, 0.4.1-2 for country-select). Step 2 (contain): If bad version confirmed, isolate the developer workstation or CI runner, kill any node.exe processes still running, and rotate any credentials present in the user's keychain or .npmrc since the payload is a token/secret stealer. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC2 (scoped relay packages on disk) and UC3 (postinstall init.js/child.js execution) on the same host to confirm payload execution; check git history of any package-lock.json the dev pushed for the same versions reaching production builds.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\node_modules\\react-native-international-phone-number\\","/node_modules/react-native-international-phone-number/","\\node_modules\\react-native-country-select\\","/node_modules/react-native-country-select/")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\node_modules\\react-native-international-phone-number\\","/node_modules/react-native-international-phone-number/","\\node_modules\\react-native-country-select\\","/node_modules/react-native-country-select/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attacker-controlled scoped npm relay packages on disk (@usebioerhold8733 / @agnoliaarisian7180) AIDelivery High
Detects creation of any file under node_modules/@usebioerhold8733/ or node_modules/@agnoliaarisian7180/. These scoped package names were registered exclusively to host the Wave-2/Wave-3 dependency-chain relay (s-format and string-argv hollow clones) and have no legitimate downstream use, making file presence essentially deterministic for compromise. Rationale: These scoped npm names (@usebioerhold8733 and @agnoliaarisian7180) were registered exclusively for the campaign per the StepSecurity disclosure (with matching Proton Mail addresses AgnoliaArisian7180@proton.me). They have zero legitimate downstream consumers, so any on-disk hit is essentially a true positive without requiring version pivot.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher staging the IOC on a sandbox VM for analysis
  • SOC threat-intel team pulling the package to enrich indicators
  • Forensic image of a previously-infected host being mounted on an investigator workstation
  • Coincidental scope collision (none known — these names were never legitimate)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host is a developer or CI environment and not a known IR/sandbox host; if confirmed prod, treat as compromise. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill node/npm processes, and capture the contents of @usebioerhold8733/s-format/init.js and child.js for IOC enrichment (postinstall, C2 hostnames, exfil targets). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same host to UC3 (postinstall hook execution) and UC4 (Solana RPC egress); search the same scope names across other hosts and the org's npm proxy/Artifactory logs for any prior pull.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\node_modules\\@usebioerhold8733\\","/node_modules/@usebioerhold8733/","\\node_modules\\@agnoliaarisian7180\\","/node_modules/@agnoliaarisian7180/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\node_modules\\@usebioerhold8733\\","/node_modules/@usebioerhold8733/","\\node_modules\\@agnoliaarisian7180\\","/node_modules/@agnoliaarisian7180/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm postinstall hook spawning node init.js or child.js (React Native attack pattern) AIInstallation Medium
Catches the moment of payload execution: npm/yarn/pnpm spawning node.exe with init.js or child.js on the command line during a package install. The article documents this exact two-step hook chain (postinstall: node child.js -> exec node init.js) inside the @usebioerhold8733/s-format payload host. Rationale: Anchors on the literal script filenames init.js and child.js called out in the article's payload dependency chain (@usebioerhold8733/s-format -> postinstall: node child.js -> exec node init.js). Constraining the parent to npm/yarn/pnpm lifecycle binaries keeps the FP rate in check while keeping coverage of the postinstall hook itself.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm package using init.js as a setup/codegen script (e.g. node-gyp, electron-builder, some create-* CLIs)
  • Custom developer monorepo scripts named init.js or child.js for project bootstrap
  • CI/CD job in a Node project that has its own lifecycle hooks executing init.js
  • One-off developer test where they wrote a script called init.js or child.js
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","electron-builder","create-react-app","create-react-native-app","create-next-app","create-vite","prebuild-install") and FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve the FolderPath of the init.js / child.js script - if it sits under node_modules/@usebioerhold8733/, node_modules/@agnoliaarisian7180/, or node_modules/react-native-international-phone-number/, treat as confirmed compromise. Step 2 (contain): Kill the node.exe process tree, isolate the host, and snapshot the script file plus any sibling .lock / config files for IR. Step 3 (hunt): Walk back to the parent npm/yarn invocation and identify which package triggered the postinstall (look at InitiatingProcessCommandLine for the package name argument); search the org for any other host that ran the same install and rotate any developer credentials that may have been in the user profile.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(init|child)\.js\b"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","cmd.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm ","yarn ","pnpm ","postinstall")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(init|child)\.js\b"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","cmd.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

node.exe contacting Solana JSON-RPC endpoints (suspected blockchain dead-drop C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts node.exe / node processes that talk to public Solana RPC endpoints - the C2 mechanism described in the article ("Solana blockchain C2 malware"). Anchors on the fact that legitimate React Native phone-input / country-select libraries have zero need to contact Solana mainnet. Rationale: Article states the payload is "Solana blockchain C2 malware". Public Solana JSON-RPC endpoints (api.mainnet-beta.solana.com plus the common RPC providers Helius / QuickNode / Alchemy / RPC Pool / Ankr) are the canonical infrastructure any Solana-blockchain dead-drop must contact. A node.exe spawned by an npm postinstall talking to these endpoints on a non-Web3 developer workstation is a sharp anomaly.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web3 developer building Solana dApps - legitimate use of @solana/web3.js
  • Crypto wallet browser extension or desktop client polling RPC endpoints
  • DevOps engineer running blockchain analytics or indexer tooling
  • Mobile dev whose React Native app legitimately integrates a Solana SDK
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","phantom.exe","solflare.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@solana/web3.js","anchor","solana-cli"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check whether the host owner has any legitimate Solana / Web3 work; if no, escalate. Resolve the contacted RPC URL and look at the raw JSON-RPC payloads in HTTP proxy logs - the C2 typically reads from a known wallet address's transaction memo / data field. Step 2 (contain): Block egress to the matched Solana RPC FQDN at the perimeter for this user; isolate the host; capture node.exe memory and the init.js / child.js scripts on disk. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC1+UC2 on the same host to confirm the compromised npm packages are present; search org-wide for other node processes contacting the same Solana RPC IPs in the last 30 days; rotate any secrets accessible from the user's profile (.npmrc tokens, ~/.aws/credentials, browser-stored creds).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("solana.com","helius-rpc","quiknode","alchemy.com","rpcpool.com","ankr.com","mainnet-beta")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("solana.com","helius-rpc","quiknode","alchemy.com","rpcpool.com","ankr.com","mainnet-beta")
| where SrcUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:*\\node.exe OR @Image:*\\Node.exe OR @Image:*\\npm.cmd OR @Image:*\\yarn.exe OR @Image:*\\pnpm.exe) (@DestinationHostname:*solana.com* OR @DestinationHostname:*helius-rpc* OR @DestinationHostname:*quiknode* OR @DestinationHostname:*alchemy.com* OR @DestinationHostname:*rpcpool.com* OR @DestinationHostname:*mainnet-beta*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(node\.exe|npm\.(cmd|exe)|yarn\.exe|pnpm\.exe)$/i
| DomainName=/(solana\.com|helius-rpc|quiknode|alchemy\.com|rpcpool\.com|mainnet-beta)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| sort - count

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Malicious Polymarket Bot Hides in Hijacked dev-protocol GitHub Org and Steals Wallet Keys

StepSecurity
2026-03-26 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The StepSecurity threat intelligence team discovered that dev-protocol — a verified GitHub organization with 568 followers belonging to a legitimate Japanese DeFi project — has been hijacked and is now being used to distribute malicious Polymarket trading bots.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious typosquat npm packages installed on disk (ts-bign / big-nunber / levex-refa / lint-builder)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Malicious Polymarket Bot Hides in Hijacked dev-protocol GitHub Org and Steals Wa
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm postinstall SSH-backdoor chain: node spawning sudo ufw allow 22/tcp + chown ~/.ssh
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 beaconing to Vercel-hosted Cloudflare-impersonating domains (cloudflareguard / cloudflareinsights) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
C2 beaconing to Vercel-hosted Cloudflare-impersonating domains (cloudflareguard / cloudflareinsights) AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound HTTP(S) traffic or DNS resolution to the two Vercel-hosted C2 domains used by the malicious dev-protocol Polymarket bot supply chain — cloudflareguard.vercel.app (wallet/file exfil) and cloudflareinsights.vercel.app (C2 config + secondary exfil). These hostnames are campaign-exclusive and have no legitimate Cloudflare provenance despite their name. Rationale: Uses the two article-specific C2 hostnames cloudflareguard.vercel.app and cloudflareinsights.vercel.app verbatim — both are campaign-exclusive impersonations of Cloudflare naming. Three external sources (StepSecurity, GetSafety, Medium ADHD/Cyb3rhawk) corroborate the C2 infrastructure. Hostnames alone are sufficient because no legitimate Cloudflare service is hosted under those Vercel subdomains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-polymarket-bot-hides-in-hijacked-dev-protocol-github-org-and-steals-wallet-keys • https://www.getsafety.com/blog-posts/polymarket-targeted-by-malicious-packages • https://medium.com/adhd-attack-detect-hunt-defend/infrastructure-pivoting-malicious-polymarket-npm-wallet-drainer-and-vidar-stealer-0b222f0e1a53
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568 T1567 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
let C2Domains = dynamic(["cloudflareguard.vercel.app","cloudflareinsights.vercel.app"]);
let C2UriPaths = dynamic(["/api/scan-patterns","/api/block-patterns","/api/v1"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(
  DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
     or (RemoteUrl has_any (C2UriPaths) and RemoteUrl has ".vercel.app")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
),
(
  DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | extend Q = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).QueryName)
  | where Q has_any (C2Domains)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Q
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["cloudflareguard.vercel.app","cloudflareinsights.vercel.app"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(
  DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Name has_any (C2Domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName
),
(
  ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (C2Domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, EventResult
),
(
  ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DstHostname has_any (C2Domains) or Url has_any (C2Domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, DstPortNumber
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Domains) or RequestURL has_any (C2Domains)
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm postinstall SSH-backdoor chain: node spawning sudo ufw allow 22/tcp + chown ~/.ssh AIInstallation High
Detects the Linux/macOS post-install backdoor sequence emitted by lint-builder's test.js — a node process (typically spawned by npm/sh in a node_modules subdirectory) invoking sudo to enable ufw, open inbound port 22/tcp, and take ownership of the SSH key directory. This sequence is the lint-builder@1.0.1 fingerprint, not generic LOLBin/SSH hardening. Rationale: References the article's exact post-install chain: 'sudo ufw allow 22/tcp', 'sudo ufw enable', 'sudo chown -R runner:runner /home/runner/.ssh', all spawned from node test.js with working directory node_modules/lint-builder. Couples the destructive command with the npm-ancestor pivot so legitimate SSH hardening (rare) doesn't fire. Corroborated by StepSecurity process tree (PIDs 2407→2422→2428→2446→2447→2449→2450) and GetSafety write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-polymarket-bot-hides-in-hijacked-dev-protocol-github-org-and-steals-wallet-keys • https://www.getsafety.com/blog-posts/polymarket-targeted-by-malicious-packages
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546.016 T1098.004 T1562.004 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let SuspectChildCmd = dynamic(["ufw allow 22","ufw allow 22/tcp","ufw enable"]);
let SshChownTokens = dynamic(["/.ssh","/home/runner/.ssh","authorized_keys"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspectChildCmd))
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "chown" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (SshChownTokens) and ProcessCommandLine has "-R")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","sh","bash","sudo","npm","dash")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node test.js","lint-builder","node_modules")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "node"
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "node_modules"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ChildFile = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          GrandparentFile = InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspectChildCmd = dynamic(["ufw allow 22","ufw allow 22/tcp","ufw enable"]);
let SshChownTokens = dynamic(["/.ssh","/home/runner/.ssh","authorized_keys"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DvcOs has "Linux" or DvcOs has "Mac" or isempty(DvcOs)
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspectChildCmd) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (SuspectChildCmd))
    or ((ActingProcessCommandLine has "chown" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "chown")
        and (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (SshChownTokens) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (SshChownTokens)))
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("node","sh","bash","sudo","npm","dash")
    or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("node test.js","lint-builder","node_modules")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node test.js","lint-builder","node_modules")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects the lint-builder@1.0.1 npm postinstall payload that opens an SSH backdoor on Linux/macOS via 'sudo ufw enable', 'sudo ufw allow 22/tcp', and 'sudo chown -R runner:runner /home/runner/.ssh', spawned from a node process executing test.js inside node_modules/lint-builder/. Part of the hijacked dev-protocol Polymarket trading bot supply chain attack (March 2026).
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-polymarket-bot-hides-in-hijacked-dev-protocol-github-org-and-steals-wallet-keys

  category: process_creation

detection:
  selection_ufw_open:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'ufw allow 22'

  selection_chown_ssh:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'chown'
      - '-R'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/.ssh'
      - '/home/runner/.ssh'
      - 'authorized_keys'
  selection_ufw_enable:
    CommandLine|contains: 'ufw enable'
  ancestry_node_npm:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/node'
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sudo'
      - '/npm'
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'node test.js'
      - 'lint-builder'
      - 'node_modules'
  condition: (selection_ufw_open or selection_chown_ssh or selection_ufw_enable) and ancestry_node_npm
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate system administrators running SSH hardening playbooks (extremely rare from a node parent)
  - Containerised CI runners installing legitimate packages that bind port 22 (audit if observed)
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:(*"ufw allow 22"* OR *"ufw allow 22/tcp"* OR *"ufw enable"* OR (*chown* AND *-R* AND (*/.ssh* OR */home/runner/.ssh* OR *authorized_keys*)))) AND (@process.parent.name:(node OR sh OR bash OR sudo OR npm OR dash) OR @process.parent.command_line:(*"node test.js"* OR *lint-builder* OR *node_modules*))

Malicious typosquat npm packages installed on disk (ts-bign / big-nunber / levex-refa / lint-builder) AIDelivery High
Hunts for filesystem evidence that any of the four named malicious npm packages from the dev-protocol Polymarket campaign were extracted under a node_modules directory. The four package names are typosquats of big.js and bignumber.js with no legitimate use — any presence in node_modules indicates a victim host that ran npm install against the hijacked repo. Rationale: All four package names (ts-bign, big-nunber, levex-refa, lint-builder) are typosquats explicitly named in the article and corroborated by GetSafety. They have no legitimate publisher on npm, so any node_modules path containing them is high-confidence evidence the host installed the malicious dev-protocol Polymarket repo. Used as a hunt-tier sweep to identify affected developer/CI hosts retroactively. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-polymarket-bot-hides-in-hijacked-dev-protocol-github-org-and-steals-wallet-keys • https://www.getsafety.com/blog-posts/polymarket-targeted-by-malicious-packages
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let MaliciousPkgs = dynamic(["ts-bign","big-nunber","levex-refa","lint-builder"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where FolderPath has_any (MaliciousPkgs)
| extend PkgName = case(
    FolderPath has "node_modules/ts-bign" or FolderPath has @"node_modules\ts-bign", "ts-bign",
    FolderPath has "node_modules/big-nunber" or FolderPath has @"node_modules\big-nunber", "big-nunber",
    FolderPath has "node_modules/levex-refa" or FolderPath has @"node_modules\levex-refa", "levex-refa",
    FolderPath has "node_modules/lint-builder" or FolderPath has @"node_modules\lint-builder", "lint-builder",
    "other")
| where PkgName != "other"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            FileCount = count(), Samples = make_set(FileName, 10),
            CreatingProcess = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5),
            CreatingCmd = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 5)
            by DeviceName, PkgName
| order by FirstSeen desc
let MaliciousPkgs = dynamic(["ts-bign","big-nunber","levex-refa","lint-builder"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (MaliciousPkgs)
| extend PkgName = case(
    TargetFilePath has "node_modules/ts-bign" or TargetFilePath has @"node_modules\ts-bign", "ts-bign",
    TargetFilePath has "node_modules/big-nunber" or TargetFilePath has @"node_modules\big-nunber", "big-nunber",
    TargetFilePath has "node_modules/levex-refa" or TargetFilePath has @"node_modules\levex-refa", "levex-refa",
    TargetFilePath has "node_modules/lint-builder" or TargetFilePath has @"node_modules\lint-builder", "lint-builder",
    "other")
| where PkgName != "other"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            FileCount = count(),
            Samples = make_set(TargetFileName, 10),
            CreatingProcess = make_set(ActingProcessName, 5)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, PkgName
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Malicious Polymarket Typosquat npm Package Files (ts-bign / big-nunber / levex-refa / lint-builder)
id: 2a9b4c7e-5d1f-4b8a-9c3e-6f7d8e2a1b09
description: Detects file creation under node_modules/ for any of the four malicious typosquat packages (ts-bign, big-nunber, levex-refa, lint-builder) distributed via the hijacked dev-protocol GitHub organization Polymarket trading bot campaign. Any presence on a development or CI host indicates that npm install was run against the malicious repo.

  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/malicious-polymarket-bot-hides-in-hijacked-dev-protocol-github-org-and-steals-wallet-keys

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1027

    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'

    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping

ForceMemo: Hundreds of GitHub Python Repos Compromised via Account Takeover and Force-Push

StepSecurity
2026-03-26 11 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The StepSecurity threat intelligence team was the first to discover and report on an ongoing campaign — which we are tracking as ForceMemo — in which an attacker is compromising hundreds of GitHub accounts and injecting identical malware into hundreds of Python repositories. The earliest injections date to March 8, 2026, and the campaign is still active with new repos continuing to be compromised.

ATT&CKT1027 T1176 T1190 T1195.002 T1204.002 T1539 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ForceMemo: Hundreds of GitHub Python Repos Compromised via Account Takeover and
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ForceMemo: Node.js v22.9.0 spawned by Python from user home directory · [LLM] ForceMemo: init.json persistence file or i.js loader dropped by Python in user home root · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ForceMemo: Python process queries Solana mainnet RPC endpoint (blockchain dead-drop C2) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
ForceMemo: Node.js v22.9.0 spawned by Python from user home directory AIInstallation High
Hunts the ForceMemo payload-execution stage where the obfuscated Python stub downloads Node.js v22.9.0 from nodejs.org, extracts it under the user's home directory, and then invokes the bundled node binary to run the AES-encrypted JS stage. A node binary inside a 'node-v22.9.0-*' folder under a user home, spawned by a python/pip parent, is highly specific to this campaign. Rationale: The 'node-v22.9.0' string is verbatim from StepSecurity's Harden-Runner capture (`/home/runner/node-v22.9.0-linux-x64/bin/node`) and is hard-coded into the malware. Pairing that path with a python/pip parent eliminates any benign Node.js installation. Cross-checked against The Hacker News, SecurityWeek and SCWorld write-ups which all reproduce the same Node.js v22.9.0 download + home-directory extraction behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/glassworm-attack-uses-stolen-github.html • https://www.securityweek.com/forcememo-python-repositories-compromised-in-glassworm-aftermath/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/glassworm-campaign-evolves-forcememo-attack-targets-python-repositories-via-stolen-github-tokens • https://www.rescana.com/post/glassworm-forcememo-campaign-supply-chain-attack-targets-github-python-repositories-with-stolen-tok/

| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python.exe","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","python3.13","pip","pip.exe","pip3")
| where FileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where FolderPath has "node-v22.9.0"
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)(\\Users\\[^\\]+\\node-v22\.9\.0-|/home/[^/]+/node-v22\.9\.0-|/Users/[^/]+/node-v22\.9\.0-|/root/node-v22\.9\.0-)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","pip","pip.exe","pip3")
| where TargetProcessName has "node-v22.9.0"
| where TargetProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(\\Users\\[^\\]+\\node-v22\.9\.0-|/home/[^/]+/node-v22\.9\.0-|/Users/[^/]+/node-v22\.9\.0-|/root/node-v22\.9\.0-)"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ForceMemo: Python process queries Solana mainnet RPC endpoint (blockchain dead-drop C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the ForceMemo blockchain C2 lookup. After execution, the malware queries the on-chain memo at Solana wallet BjVeAjPrSKFiingBn4vZvghsGj9KCE8AJVtbc9S8o8SC via one of 9 named Solana RPC providers, fetching its current payload URL. A Python (or pip) process contacting any of these RPC endpoints is high-fidelity for non-crypto orgs. Rationale: All 9 RPC FQDNs are verbatim from the StepSecurity write-up and are hard-coded in the malware as a resilient fallback chain. The Solana C2 wallet (BjVeAjPrSKF...8o8SC) is corroborated on-chain and across The Hacker News / SecurityWeek / SCWorld / Rescana. Pairing the destination with a python/pip parent removes the only realistic FP class (legit Web3 devs). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/glassworm-attack-uses-stolen-github.html • https://www.securityweek.com/forcememo-python-repositories-compromised-in-glassworm-aftermath/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/glassworm-forcememo-campaign-supply-chain-attack-targets-github-python-repositories-with-stolen-tok/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/forcememo-hijacks-github-accounts/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution Network_Traffic

union
  ( DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python.exe","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","python3.13","pip","pip.exe","pip3")
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (SolanaRpc)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="Network", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName ),
  ( DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python.exe","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","python3.13","pip","pip.exe","pip3")
    | extend Query = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).QueryName)
    | where Query in~ (SolanaRpc)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="DNS", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl=Query, RemoteIP, RemotePort=int(null), AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName )
| order by Timestamp desc

ForceMemo: init.json persistence file or i.js loader dropped by Python in user home root AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ForceMemo persistence and JS-loader artefacts. The Python stub writes a JavaScript decryption loader as 'i.js' and a 'init.json' state file with a 2-day recheck timer directly into the user's home directory root. Both filenames are short and generic, but the combination of (python/pip parent) + (filename) + (path = home-directory root, not nested) is highly specific. Rationale: Filenames 'i.js' and 'init.json' and their direct-in-home-root location are verbatim from the StepSecurity write-up ('Writes a JS file (i.js)... Creates a persistence file (~/init.json) with a 2-day recheck timer'). The (python parent) + (home-root, not nested) regex eliminates almost all benign 'init.json' creations, which typically live in app-config or package subdirs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/glassworm-attack-uses-stolen-github.html • https://www.securityweek.com/forcememo-python-repositories-compromised-in-glassworm-aftermath/ • https://gbhackers.com/forcememo-hijacks-github/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python.exe","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","python3.13","pip","pip.exe","pip3")
| where FileName in~ ("init.json","i.js")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)^([A-Z]:\\Users\\[^\\]+\\?|/home/[^/]+/?|/Users/[^/]+/?|/root/?)$"
| where FolderPath !has "site-packages" and FolderPath !has "node_modules" and FolderPath !has ".venv" and FolderPath !has "venv"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","pip","pip.exe","pip3")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("init.json","i.js")
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)^([A-Z]:\\Users\\[^\\]+\\(init\.json|i\.js)|/home/[^/]+/(init\.json|i\.js)|/Users/[^/]+/(init\.json|i\.js)|/root/(init\.json|i\.js))$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027

    - attack.defense-evasion

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high

      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

xygeni-action Compromised: C2 Reverse Shell Backdoor Injected via Tag Poisoning

StepSecurity
2026-03-26 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The official Xygeni GitHub Action (xygeni-action) was compromised on March 3, 2026, when an attacker using stolen maintainer credentials injected a full C2 reverse shell backdoor and silently moved the mutable v5 tag to the malicious commit - affecting all repositories referencing @v5 without any visible change to their workflow files. The v5 tag remains poisoned as of March 9; users should immediately pin to v6.4.0 or a specific commit SHA, and StepSecurity's Harden-Runner would have detected and blocked the C2 callback to 91.214.78.178.

Outbound C2 callback to xygeni-action backdoor IP 91.214.78.178 from CI runner AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any outbound connection from a host (typically a CI/CD runner) to the xygeni-action C2 infrastructure: the literal IP 91.214.78.178 or any nip.io wildcard subdomain wrapping that IP (e.g. security-verify.91.214.78.178.nip.io). The implant registers via POST /b/in then polls /b/q every 2-7s for 3 minutes. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim C2 IP (91.214.78.178) and the nip.io wildcard FQDN (security-verify.91.214.78.178.nip.io) named in the article. The IP belongs to attacker-controlled infrastructure and nip.io subdomains embedding that IP only exist for the purpose of evading IP-block lists; no legitimate enterprise traffic should resolve them. Cross-checked with StepSecurity's incident write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/xygeni-action-compromised-c2-reverse-shell-backdoor-injected-via-tag-poisoning
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090 T1568.002

  • Security researchers issuing manual curl probes to 91.214.78.178 from a known analyst jump-box
  • Allowed-listed external scanners (Shodan, Censys, GreyNoise) hitting outbound DNS for nip.io domains during reconnaissance studies
  • TI feed validators verifying that the IOC is reachable
  • SOAR playbooks performing an active-test connection to the IOC

| where not(DeviceName has_any ("soc-research-", "ti-sandbox-", "redteam-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on the offending Host/aid - identify whether it is a GitHub Actions self-hosted runner, GitHub-hosted runner egressing via an enterprise NAT, or a developer workstation. Pull all DeviceProcessEvents / ImProcessCreate within +/- 5 min of the network hit to confirm the parent was a bash subshell from the action checkout. 2) Contain: block egress to 91.214.78.178/32 and *.91.214.78.178.nip.io at the proxy/firewall; if the host is a runner, take it offline immediately and rotate every secret the runner had access to (GITHUB_TOKEN, XYGENI_TOKEN, cloud OIDC tokens, deploy keys). 3) Hunt: scan repository workflow YAML for any reference to xygeni/xygeni-action@v5 or @4bf1d4e (PR/CI history too); review GitHub audit log for token-pulls and write-events from the runner during the C2 window; correlate against any anomalous git push or release artifact upload.

GitHub Actions workflow file referencing compromised xygeni/xygeni-action@v5 or backdoored commit 4bf1d4e AIDelivery High
Detects on-disk evidence that a self-hosted runner has checked out (or that a developer workstation has cloned) the xygeni/xygeni-action repo at the poisoned v5 tag or the backdoored commit 4bf1d4e from PR #48, prior to or independent of network detection. Pre-execution catch. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim repo path (xygeni/xygeni-action), the poisoned mutable tag (v5), and the backdoored commit SHA prefix (4bf1d4e) explicitly named in the article. Excludes the post-incident clean release (commit 13c6ed2 / v6.4.0) and the legitimate frozen v5.38.1 release to suppress benign reads of the same repo. Cross-checked with the StepSecurity tag-state inventory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/xygeni-action-compromised-c2-reverse-shell-backdoor-injected-via-tag-poisoning
